title: Anthropic Adds a Claude Code Rule on Opus 5.5 That Blocks Recreations of Existing Games
summary: Anthropic has added a rule to Claude Code, its AI coding assistant, that stops the tool from recreating specific existing video games when it runs on the Opus 5.5 model. Anthropic confirmed the change through a post by Addy Osmani, a member of its technical staff, who said the company added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from rebuilding someone else's game. The rule reached Claude Code around October 27, according to X user Chasm, who first shared the change. Chasm reports that the instruction is delivered from Anthropic's servers under a flag named "tengu_heron_brook" and that users cannot switch it off. What the New Claude Code Rule Allows and Blocks The instruction tells Claude to keep building original games, games in an established genre, and games based on the user's own designs and assets. Recreating a specific existing game is off the table, and the rule says this applies "even if it is renamed or called original." In practice, the rule draws this line: allowed: original game concepts, genre games, and projects built from the developer's own designs and assets blocked: a copy of a specific existing game, including versions that carry a new name or are described as original Osmani says the reason is Anthropic's usage policy, which already prohibits using Claude to infringe intellectual property. The prompt change makes Claude Code enforce that policy directly when a request targets a particular game. Anthropic says it will continue to adjust the rule to strike the right balance. Osmani asked developers whose own projects are refused by Claude to send those cases to him directly. Why Anthropic Is Targeting AI Game Clones The change follows complaints about low-effort AI-generated games during Valve's Steam Next Fest in October. Players reported that their feeds filled up with clones of existing games, including copies of titles that had only just released their own demos. Some developers reacted by pulling public demos. The team behind Drunken Goddess Reflux, Alliance Arts and Who You, canceled its Steam demo plans in favor of private playtests. Valve responded that it would be "thinking about how to solve this problem." For developers who use Claude Code, the practical impact depends on the project. Original work and genre games should continue to work as before. Requests to reproduce a known game, or to rebuild one under a new title, now fail on Opus 5.5. Anthropic's previous Claude launch, the Claude Duet background agent , was limited to paying subscribers, while the game rule is applied server-side to Claude Code on Opus 5.5 with no user setting to disable it. Anthropic has not said whether a specific incident prompted the change, whether the rule will extend to other Claude models, or how it treats mods, decompilations, and recompilations of existing games. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.

Anthropic has added a rule to Claude Code, its AI coding assistant, that stops the tool from recreating specific existing video games when it runs on the Opus 5.5 model.

Anthropic confirmed the change through a post by Addy Osmani, a member of its technical staff, who said the company added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from rebuilding someone else's game.

The rule reached Claude Code around October 27, according to X user Chasm, who first shared the change. Chasm reports that the instruction is delivered from Anthropic's servers under a flag named "tengu_heron_brook" and that users cannot switch it off.

What the New Claude Code Rule Allows and Blocks

The instruction tells Claude to keep building original games, games in an established genre, and games based on the user's own designs and assets. Recreating a specific existing game is off the table, and the rule says this applies "even if it is renamed or called original."

In practice, the rule draws this line:

  • allowed: original game concepts, genre games, and projects built from the developer's own designs and assets
  • blocked: a copy of a specific existing game, including versions that carry a new name or are described as original

Osmani says the reason is Anthropic's usage policy, which already prohibits using Claude to infringe intellectual property. The prompt change makes Claude Code enforce that policy directly when a request targets a particular game.

Anthropic says it will continue to adjust the rule to strike the right balance. Osmani asked developers whose own projects are refused by Claude to send those cases to him directly.

Why Anthropic Is Targeting AI Game Clones

The change follows complaints about low-effort AI-generated games during Valve's Steam Next Fest in October. Players reported that their feeds filled up with clones of existing games, including copies of titles that had only just released their own demos.

Some developers reacted by pulling public demos. The team behind Drunken Goddess Reflux, Alliance Arts and Who You, canceled its Steam demo plans in favor of private playtests. Valve responded that it would be "thinking about how to solve this problem."

For developers who use Claude Code, the practical impact depends on the project. Original work and genre games should continue to work as before. Requests to reproduce a known game, or to rebuild one under a new title, now fail on Opus 5.5. Anthropic's previous Claude launch, the Claude Duet background agent, was limited to paying subscribers, while the game rule is applied server-side to Claude Code on Opus 5.5 with no user setting to disable it.

Anthropic has not said whether a specific incident prompted the change, whether the rule will extend to other Claude models, or how it treats mods, decompilations, and recompilations of existing games.

title: AI translation sounds convincing, but it can be riddled with hidden errors
summary: Jorg Greuel/Getty Images Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are more widespread than ever, and one of the functions they offer is fast, real-time translation. Some people are even questioning the need to ever learn another language , if near-instant translation is so widely available to all of us, often for free. However, those translations are far from perfect. While AI translations are very fluent, fluency doesn’t equal accuracy. Even proficient bilinguals can overlook errors hidden under the surface . Some of the mistakes in AI translation come from a lack of learning data, insufficient prompts, or even hallucations – confident presentation of false information, a hallmark of AI chatbots. Other errors reflect something more fundamental: the inherent complexity and flexibility of human language, and the linguistic or cultural differences between two languages. In my professional work reviewing real AI translations between English and Chinese, I have found some revealing examples of this problem. English and Chinese are two of the most used languages , with a large amount of data for AI to learn from; the issues could be more serious if you’re working on less common languages . For those using generative AI to translate, it’s important to keep these risks in mind. Where can AI translation go wrong? At word level Words can have multiple meanings and AI may not always choose the right one. In one translation I reviewed, an international student described Australian professors as laid back because they wore thongs to class. AI interpreted “thongs” as G-strings (underwear) rather than flip-flops (footwear). Tense can be problematic too. English verbs clearly indicate tense through forms such as “go”, “went” and “is going”. Chinese verbs don’t change in the same way. Instead, time is often conveyed through context or other words. When translating Chinese into English, AI can choose the wrong tense, changing whether something has happened, is happening or will happen. At sentence level A sentence can have different interpretations that are grammatically correct but different in meaning. For example, “You can see him in the store” can mean he is in the store – or you’re in the store when you see him. A human translator can often resolve such ambiguity by considering the context, but AI makes a decision by predicting the next possible words. And if a mistake is made, it can be difficult to spot later when the overall AI output sounds completely natural. Without careful checking against the original, the meaning can be changed without you noticing. At whole text level Accuracy involves more than getting individual words and sentences right. Information must also flow across a text, which is known as cohesion. And languages often achieve cohesion differently. For example, English frequently uses definite article “the” to refer back to something previously mentioned. “The” doesn’t exist in Chinese; cohesion is achieved by repeating the same word over and over throughout the text. AI can sometimes connect these references incorrectly, leaving readers confused about who or what is being discussed. Beyond communicating information Language doesn’t just communicate information. People also use it to establish relationships and connect with others. Different languages and cultures can build similar relationships in different ways, depending on cultural or ideological differences. For example, government communications in Australia often use “we” and “you” to build a closer relationship with the general public. By contrast, another language – such as Chinese – may prefer third person and more formal words for distance and authority. Translation is also about introducing new ideas to another language or reflecting evolving beliefs about existing expressions. For example, terms such as “ neurodiversity ” may not have widely established equivalents in another language. And when communities want to address stigma inherent to certain expressions, they might intentionally replace previously used words with new and emerging ones. For example, Chinese terminology referring to transgender people has evolved – more inclusive expressions are gaining recognition . AI may reproduce older or less appropriate terminology, particularly where newer expressions are underrepresented in its training data. A translation can therefore be linguistically understandable yet socially insensitive. So when can you trust AI translation? Just as AI is a black box, your AI translation is also a black box. No large language model can guarantee your AI translation always comes out perfectly. But overall, AI translation tends to be more reliable when: the topic is familiar and straightforward across two languages, not involving cultural difference or sensitive issues the original text is written in perfect grammar and clear sentence structure with no ambiguity the two languages are both among most widely used languages (such as English, Chinese, French or Spanish), which means more training data is available for AI to learn from you provide effective prompts: clearly define the context, the reader, the purpose, and the language features of the translation task. The translation provided by a chatbot will also be more accurate if it’s combined with neural machine translation technology – this is AI that’s dedicated to translation specifically and trained accordingly. It’s not a feature usually available on the common free AI platforms. However, even when all the boxes are ticked, accuracy can’t be guaranteed; errors can crop up, hallucinations can happen . You trust it at your own risk. Remember, generative AI doesn’t truly understand the complex and often ambiguous human experiences in a text. It may be good enough for understanding the general idea of a text, but its quality is never guaranteed without human input. summary_html:
Jorg Greuel/Getty Images

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are more widespread than ever, and one of the functions they offer is fast, real-time translation. Some people are even questioning the need to ever learn another language, if near-instant translation is so widely available to all of us, often for free.

However, those translations are far from perfect. While AI translations are very fluent, fluency doesn’t equal accuracy. Even proficient bilinguals can overlook errors hidden under the surface.

Some of the mistakes in AI translation come from a lack of learning data, insufficient prompts, or even hallucations – confident presentation of false information, a hallmark of AI chatbots.

Other errors reflect something more fundamental: the inherent complexity and flexibility of human language, and the linguistic or cultural differences between two languages.

In my professional work reviewing real AI translations between English and Chinese, I have found some revealing examples of this problem. English and Chinese are two of the most used languages, with a large amount of data for AI to learn from; the issues could be more serious if you’re working on less common languages.

For those using generative AI to translate, it’s important to keep these risks in mind.

Where can AI translation go wrong?

At word level

Words can have multiple meanings and AI may not always choose the right one.

In one translation I reviewed, an international student described Australian professors as laid back because they wore thongs to class. AI interpreted “thongs” as G-strings (underwear) rather than flip-flops (footwear).

Tense can be problematic too. English verbs clearly indicate tense through forms such as “go”, “went” and “is going”. Chinese verbs don’t change in the same way. Instead, time is often conveyed through context or other words. When translating Chinese into English, AI can choose the wrong tense, changing whether something has happened, is happening or will happen.

At sentence level

A sentence can have different interpretations that are grammatically correct but different in meaning.

For example, “You can see him in the store” can mean he is in the store – or you’re in the store when you see him. A human translator can often resolve such ambiguity by considering the context, but AI makes a decision by predicting the next possible words.

And if a mistake is made, it can be difficult to spot later when the overall AI output sounds completely natural. Without careful checking against the original, the meaning can be changed without you noticing.

At whole text level

Accuracy involves more than getting individual words and sentences right. Information must also flow across a text, which is known as cohesion. And languages often achieve cohesion differently.

For example, English frequently uses definite article “the” to refer back to something previously mentioned. “The” doesn’t exist in Chinese; cohesion is achieved by repeating the same word over and over throughout the text.

AI can sometimes connect these references incorrectly, leaving readers confused about who or what is being discussed.

Beyond communicating information

Language doesn’t just communicate information. People also use it to establish relationships and connect with others.

Different languages and cultures can build similar relationships in different ways, depending on cultural or ideological differences. For example, government communications in Australia often use “we” and “you” to build a closer relationship with the general public. By contrast, another language – such as Chinese – may prefer third person and more formal words for distance and authority.

Translation is also about introducing new ideas to another language or reflecting evolving beliefs about existing expressions.

For example, terms such as “neurodiversity” may not have widely established equivalents in another language.

And when communities want to address stigma inherent to certain expressions, they might intentionally replace previously used words with new and emerging ones. For example, Chinese terminology referring to transgender people has evolved – more inclusive expressions are gaining recognition.

AI may reproduce older or less appropriate terminology, particularly where newer expressions are underrepresented in its training data. A translation can therefore be linguistically understandable yet socially insensitive.

So when can you trust AI translation?

Just as AI is a black box, your AI translation is also a black box. No large language model can guarantee your AI translation always comes out perfectly. But overall, AI translation tends to be more reliable when:

  • the topic is familiar and straightforward across two languages, not involving cultural difference or sensitive issues

  • the original text is written in perfect grammar and clear sentence structure with no ambiguity

  • the two languages are both among most widely used languages (such as English, Chinese, French or Spanish), which means more training data is available for AI to learn from

  • you provide effective prompts: clearly define the context, the reader, the purpose, and the language features of the translation task.

The translation provided by a chatbot will also be more accurate if it’s combined with neural machine translation technology – this is AI that’s dedicated to translation specifically and trained accordingly. It’s not a feature usually available on the common free AI platforms.

However, even when all the boxes are ticked, accuracy can’t be guaranteed; errors can crop up, hallucinations can happen. You trust it at your own risk.

Remember, generative AI doesn’t truly understand the complex and often ambiguous human experiences in a text. It may be good enough for understanding the general idea of a text, but its quality is never guaranteed without human input.

title: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file
summary: I've been getting the occasional confusing Python dependency error since switching over to Python 3.15 and the rule I'm having to remember is: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file Most of my projects are libraries which don't include a uv.lock file, since it's rude for a library dependency to lock versions for anything else that uses it. Running uv run pytest etc tends to leave uv.lock files lying around, which are listed in .gitignore and so do not get committed to my repositories. But... sometimes that uv.lock pins a version of a dependency that doesn't yet have a Python 3.15 wheel. An example from earlier today: error: Failed to build `watchfiles==1.1.1` cause: Call to `maturin.build_wheel` failed error: the configured Python interpreter version (3.15) is newer than PyO3's maximum supported version (3.14) Deleting that file and running uv run pytest again usually fixes the problem. Tags: uv , til , python
summary_html:
I've been getting the occasional confusing Python dependency error since switching over to Python 3.15 and the rule I'm having to remember is:

If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file

Most of my projects are libraries which don't include a uv.lock file, since it's rude for a library dependency to lock versions for anything else that uses it.

Running uv run pytest etc tends to leave uv.lock files lying around, which are listed in .gitignore and so do not get committed to my repositories.

But... sometimes that uv.lock pins a version of a dependency that doesn't yet have a Python 3.15 wheel. An example from earlier today:

error: Failed to build `watchfiles==1.1.1`
  cause: Call to `maturin.build_wheel` failed

error: the configured Python interpreter version (3.15) is newer
than PyO3's maximum supported version (3.14)

Deleting that file and running uv run pytest again usually fixes the problem.

Tags: uv, til, python
source: Simon Willison's Weblog

title: Apple, Uber and Elections Headline Week
summary: Can Apple, Uber and Palantir turn this stock market around? It sure needs it. Worries about excessive AI spending tanked Google’s stock last week and sent the Nasdaq Composite to its worst month since March 2025. While the major indexes are still in the green for the year, a few more days like Friday’s could change that. Fortunately, we have a handful of earnings that might temper the gloom. Palantir Technologies, which reports Monday, has told investors to expect an 83% jump in the third quarter from the year-ago period. That’s a slowdown from the second quarter’s blistering 93% growth . But at least investors will get a reprieve from enormous capital expenditures. Palantir only spent $22 million in capex in the first half. As for Apple, it’s already warned investors that supply constraints for advanced chip manufacturing would contribute to slower revenue growth, to a range of 9% to 11% in the September quarter from a year ago, slower than its 16% growth in the June quarter. Apple has also forecast iPhone revenue growth in the mid-teens versus 22% in the June quarter. An improvement on that outlook could buoy the mood. On the other hand, a sharper slowdown in growth from either companies could give investors another reason to sell tech stocks.

title: OpenAI wants everyone to call AI data centers 'compute campuses'
summary: OpenAI has a new, more chic name for data centers. Bloomberg/Getty Images OpenAI wants to rebrand AI data centers using a new, more alliterative name. "Compute campuses" is their new-fangled term. An OpenAI spokesperson said it better represents the "role" of AI infrastructure. OpenAI doesn't want to call them " data centers " anymore. Instead, the ChatGPT maker plans to propose a new, more chic name for the behemoth factories that power your chatbot queries. That new name is "compute campuses," an OpenAI spokesperson confirmed to Business Insider on Sunday. "Compute campuses better describes the scale and role of the infrastructure we're building for AI," the spokesperson said. "These are long-term investments in computing, energy infrastructure and skilled work." Though much has been said about the less-than-stellar reputations of AI data centers (a recent Pew Research poll found that 54% of Americans say AI data centers are bad for the environment), efforts to ameliorate that view have mostly failed. Data centers are now a major issue for voters in the midterms. While major data center builders like Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft have pledged millions of dollars to the communities and schools surrounding their centers, OpenAI is betting that a complete rebrand will also help turn around public opinion. "We want the communities hosting that infrastructure to help shape it and share in the opportunities it creates," the OpenAI spokesperson said. Time will tell, however, if the "compute campus" lingo catches on. Axios earlier reported that OpenAI was also preparing for a blue wave in Tuesday's midterm elections, which could result in a more regulatory-minded government. title: Elon Musk says he is taking over an old Spam factory and a gun range to expand his Colossus 2 AI complex
summary: Elon Musk said his company and contractors are making "good progress" at the Colossus 2 site. Finn Gomez/Getty Images Elon Musk is expanding Colossus 2 in Tennessee. Musk said two additional facilities, Spam and Gun Range, will be operational before 2027. Last week, a judge rejected SpaceX's motion to dismiss a lawsuit filed by the NAACP over Colossus 2. Elon Musk isn't wasting any time building out his massive AI-computing facilities in Tennessee. Musk said on X that he's expanding Colossus 2 with two additional sites, dubbed Spam and Gun Range. He said the Spam location used to house Hormel-brand products, Spam perhaps among them , and that the Gun Range location was once owned by the local police department. "I walked the whole Colossus 2 site around midnight and again this morning. Good progress by the SpaceX team and contractors," Musk said on X. "Gun Range is tracking to be operational by end of November and Spam in December." Developing and running AI systems requires enormous amounts of compute power, which led Musk to build a supercomputer called Colossus in Memphis in 2024. xAI, acquired by SpaceX, later expanded the project with Colossus 2 to generate more power for its AI chatbot, Grok. Construction for that campus began last year in Memphis. Supercomputers and data centers are necessary to power AI systems, though they've often drawn ire from communities where the hulking facilities are built. Colossus and Colossus 2 are no different. Residents near Memphis have packed public hearings, staged protests, and created petitions opposing the campuses. In April, the NAACP filed a lawsuit against xAI and its subsidiary, MZX Tech, saying they were unlawfully operating unpermitted methane gas turbines to power Colossus 2. The complaint said xAI was operating the unpermitted gas turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, which is less than 20 minutes away. Last week, a US District Judge denied xAI and MZX Tech's motion to dismiss the lawsuit. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Giving an AI agent a wallet without giving it your keys
summary: Agents are starting to pay for things. An agent buying API credits, renting a GPU for an hour or paying for a dataset is no longer a thought experiment, and x402 (HTTP 402 Payment Required with on-chain payment) makes it a normal web request. That leaves the question of how the agent holds money. The two bad options Give the agent a private key. It works until a prompt injection, a bug or a leaked environment file. Then the wallet is empty, and there is nothing between the key and the funds. Approve every payment by hand. Safe, and it removes the reason to use an agent. What people actually want is what they already do with a company card: a limit per purchase, a monthly budget, a list of places it works, and a phone call for anything unusual. Put the limits where the agent can't reach them The limits have to live somewhere the agent, and the machine it runs on, can't change. A smart contract is a good fit: the rules are checked by every node, and changing them needs the owner's key. Purser is an ERC-4337 smart account built for this. The owner grants each agent a session key with a policy: an allow-list of contracts and functions it may call a cap per payment and a budget per period, per token a validity window Inside the policy, the agent pays on its own. Over the limit, the payment becomes an approval request, and it runs only if the owner co-signs. One transaction revokes a key or freezes the whole account. If the agent's key leaks, the damage is bounded: the rest of the current budget, at allowed places, until you revoke it. The part that was harder than it looks ERC-4337 splits an operation into validation and execution, and validation is not allowed to read the clock (ERC-7562), because bundlers have to be able to simulate it reliably. A daily budget is all about the clock. So the checks are split: Validation: signature, validity window, allow-list and per-payment cap. A disallowed call fails here, before it costs anything. Execution: the rolling budget, in executeUserOp , where reading the block time is fine. Two smaller rules that matter: an owner approval raises the amount but never the scope, so an approved payment still has to be to an allowed place; and a revoke earlier in a bundle still stops a later operation in the same bundle. Testing money code Unit tests aren't enough for this. Purser has 41 unit tests through a real EntryPoint, fuzz tests that compare random payment and time sequences against a simple model of the budget, and invariant tests that throw thousands of random calls at the account and check three properties after each one: no spending over budget without approval, no funds moved by a revoked key, no policy change without the owner. Slither runs in CI. It's still early and not audited, which is why everything below runs on a local chain. Agents use it through MCP An MCP server exposes six tools: wallet_status , send_eth , send_token , call_contract , get_request and list_requests . Each payment returns one of three outcomes, written for the model: done with the budget left, waiting for the owner with a request id, or refused with a reason it can act on. Try it docker run --rm -it -p 127.0.0.1:8787:8787 ghcr.io/ahmad-codex/purser:demo Open http://localhost:8787 . The container starts a local chain, deploys everything, and plays the agent story while the console updates. Then connect your own agent: claude mcp add --transport http purser http://localhost:8787/mcp and ask it to pay the merchant 0.3 ETH. The roadmap starts with paying x402 endpoints within the budget, a gas budget per key and EIP-7702 support. It's MIT licensed, and there are good first issues open. If you let agents spend money today, I'd like to hear how you limit it.
summary_html:
Agents are starting to pay for things. An agent buying API credits, renting a GPU for an hour or paying for a dataset is no longer a thought experiment, and x402 (HTTP 402 Payment Required with on-chain payment) makes it a normal web request.

That leaves the question of how the agent holds money.

The two bad options

Give the agent a private key. It works until a prompt injection, a bug or a leaked environment file. Then the wallet is empty, and there is nothing between the key and the funds.

Approve every payment by hand. Safe, and it removes the reason to use an agent.

What people actually want is what they already do with a company card: a limit per purchase, a monthly budget, a list of places it works, and a phone call for anything unusual.

Put the limits where the agent can't reach them

The limits have to live somewhere the agent, and the machine it runs on, can't change. A smart contract is a good fit: the rules are checked by every node, and changing them needs the owner's key.

Purser is an ERC-4337 smart account built for this. The owner grants each agent a session key with a policy:

  • an allow-list of contracts and functions it may call
  • a cap per payment and a budget per period, per token
  • a validity window

Inside the policy, the agent pays on its own. Over the limit, the payment becomes an approval request, and it runs only if the owner co-signs. One transaction revokes a key or freezes the whole account.

If the agent's key leaks, the damage is bounded: the rest of the current budget, at allowed places, until you revoke it.

The part that was harder than it looks

ERC-4337 splits an operation into validation and execution, and validation is not allowed to read the clock (ERC-7562), because bundlers have to be able to simulate it reliably. A daily budget is all about the clock.

So the checks are split:

  • Validation: signature, validity window, allow-list and per-payment cap. A disallowed call fails here, before it costs anything.
  • Execution: the rolling budget, in executeUserOp, where reading the block time is fine.

Two smaller rules that matter: an owner approval raises the amount but never the scope, so an approved payment still has to be to an allowed place; and a revoke earlier in a bundle still stops a later operation in the same bundle.

Testing money code

Unit tests aren't enough for this. Purser has 41 unit tests through a real EntryPoint, fuzz tests that compare random payment and time sequences against a simple model of the budget, and invariant tests that throw thousands of random calls at the account and check three properties after each one: no spending over budget without approval, no funds moved by a revoked key, no policy change without the owner. Slither runs in CI.

It's still early and not audited, which is why everything below runs on a local chain.

Agents use it through MCP

An MCP server exposes six tools: wallet_status, send_eth, send_token, call_contract, get_request and list_requests. Each payment returns one of three outcomes, written for the model: done with the budget left, waiting for the owner with a request id, or refused with a reason it can act on.

Try it 
docker run --rm -it -p 127.0.0.1:8787:8787 ghcr.io/ahmad-codex/purser:demo

Open http://localhost:8787. The container starts a local chain, deploys everything, and plays the agent story while the console updates. Then connect your own agent:

claude mcp add --transport http purser http://localhost:8787/mcp

and ask it to pay the merchant 0.3 ETH.

The roadmap starts with paying x402 endpoints within the budget, a gas budget per key and EIP-7702 support. It's MIT licensed, and there are good first issues open. If you let agents spend money today, I'd like to hear how you limit it.

title: I Fact-Checked Every Finding an AI Security Reviewer Gave Me. Here's What Held Up.
summary: During my internship at RakFort, one of my tasks was simple to describe and slow to do: run every security check in Secfoo with the Claude agent, and then check whether the AI was actually right. Not "did the run finish". Not "does the report look good". Is each finding true ? This post is about what I found, and what I'd tell anyone who is starting to use AI for security reviews. Quick background: what Secfoo is Secfoo is an open-source tool that turns the AI coding agent you already use (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and others) into a security reviewer. You point it at your code, pick a check, and it gives the AI clear instructions and a fixed report format. You get back a structured report with findings, severity and recommendations, and everything shows up in a local dashboard. secfoo run --skill deployment-readiness --agent claude --target . secfoo serve # open the dashboard It has 9 checks, including SAST, threat modeling, secret scanning, dependency triage, deployment readiness and responsible AI compliance. How I tested My target was Secfoo's own codebase (a good test, because I could read every file the AI talked about). For each report I: Opened every finding Went to the exact file and line it pointed to Checked the code as it was on the day of the scan (using the commit from that date, not today's code) Marked it Confirmed , Partly wrong or Wrong Checked that the numbers on the dashboard matched the report Step 3 matters more than I expected. Code changes every day. If you check an old report against today's code, you'll blame the AI for things that were true at the time. Results Deployment readiness: 6 of 7 fully correct # Severity Finding Verdict F1 High Local dashboard has no login or CSRF protection ✅ Confirmed (exact lines were right) F2 High No security scanning in CI ⚠️ Partly wrong F3 Medium Release actions pinned by tag, long-lived tokens ✅ Confirmed F4 Medium Uploads saved to disk before the size check ✅ Confirmed F5 Medium Docker image runs as root, base image not pinned ✅ Confirmed F6 Low No health endpoint ✅ Confirmed F7 Low Dependencies have no upper version pins ✅ Confirmed Responsible AI compliance: 4 of 4 correct All four findings were accurate, and the overall rating ("Low") made sense for a tool that doesn't make decisions about people. The interesting one: F2 Most of F2 was right. CI really didn't run any security scanners, and the linter was set to never fail the build. But the report also said the release workflow "runs on any v* tag push" . It didn't. The workflow had been changed to manual-only five days before the scan. The file even had a comment at the top explaining the change. So the AI described how the project used to work. My guess is that it matched a very common pattern ("release on tag push") instead of reading the current trigger carefully. This is exactly the kind of mistake that is easy to miss: It sounds completely reasonable It's in a well-formatted report next to six correct findings It's only wrong in one detail If I had just skimmed the report, I would have believed it. Things I tested besides the reports Bad input. I fed the CLI things a real user might get wrong: a folder that doesn't exist, a file instead of a folder, an unknown skill or agent name, a GitHub repo that doesn't exist. Every one gave a clear error, with no crash and no AI tokens wasted. I found two small issues (a negative --timeout was accepted, and an empty target quietly scanned the current folder) and reported them. The dashboard. All pages loaded and the finding counts matched the reports, except the home page, which crashed with a 500 error. The cause was a recent change: agents that don't report cost now store "unknown" instead of $0, and the home page added the costs together with a plain sum() , which fails on an empty value. It was a one-line fix, and my PR for it ( #31 ) is now merged. What I learned 1. AI reviewers are genuinely useful. Most findings were correct, with the right file and line numbers. For coverage and speed, it's a huge help, especially for a small team. 2. "Looks professional" is not the same as "true". The one wrong detail was written just as confidently as the correct ones. Severity labels and neat tables don't make a finding correct. 3. Check against the right version of the code. Use the commit from the scan date. Otherwise you'll mark correct findings as wrong (or the other way round). 4. Keep a human in the loop for anything that matters. If a report is going to someone who will sign it off, every finding should be checked first. It took me a while, but it's much faster than reviewing the code from scratch. Try it Secfoo is free and open source (MIT). If you're a student or developer interested in security, try it on your own project and check the findings yourself. That's honestly the best way to learn what AI reviewers are good and bad at. 👉 https://github.com/secfoo-com/secfoo Feedback, issues and contributions are welcome. I'd love to hear how it does on your code! This is my second post about Secfoo. The first one was about catching an AI scanner inventing fake vulnerabilities . security #ai #opensource #testing
summary_html:
During my internship at RakFort, one of my tasks was simple to describe and slow to do: run every security check in Secfoo with the Claude agent, and then check whether the AI was actually right.

Not "did the run finish". Not "does the report look good". Is each finding true?

This post is about what I found, and what I'd tell anyone who is starting to use AI for security reviews.

Quick background: what Secfoo is

Secfoo is an open-source tool that turns the AI coding agent you already use (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and others) into a security reviewer.

You point it at your code, pick a check, and it gives the AI clear instructions and a fixed report format. You get back a structured report with findings, severity and recommendations, and everything shows up in a local dashboard.

secfoo run --skill deployment-readiness --agent claude --target .
secfoo serve   # open the dashboard

It has 9 checks, including SAST, threat modeling, secret scanning, dependency triage, deployment readiness and responsible AI compliance.

How I tested

My target was Secfoo's own codebase (a good test, because I could read every file the AI talked about).

For each report I:

  1. Opened every finding
  2. Went to the exact file and line it pointed to
  3. Checked the code as it was on the day of the scan (using the commit from that date, not today's code)
  4. Marked it Confirmed, Partly wrong or Wrong
  5. Checked that the numbers on the dashboard matched the report

Step 3 matters more than I expected. Code changes every day. If you check an old report against today's code, you'll blame the AI for things that were true at the time.

Results Deployment readiness: 6 of 7 fully correct
# Severity Finding Verdict F1 High Local dashboard has no login or CSRF protection ✅ Confirmed (exact lines were right) F2 High No security scanning in CI ⚠️ Partly wrong F3 Medium Release actions pinned by tag, long-lived tokens ✅ Confirmed F4 Medium Uploads saved to disk before the size check ✅ Confirmed F5 Medium Docker image runs as root, base image not pinned ✅ Confirmed F6 Low No health endpoint ✅ Confirmed F7 Low Dependencies have no upper version pins ✅ Confirmed
Responsible AI compliance: 4 of 4 correct

All four findings were accurate, and the overall rating ("Low") made sense for a tool that doesn't make decisions about people.

The interesting one: F2

Most of F2 was right. CI really didn't run any security scanners, and the linter was set to never fail the build.

But the report also said the release workflow "runs on any v* tag push".

It didn't. The workflow had been changed to manual-only five days before the scan. The file even had a comment at the top explaining the change.

So the AI described how the project used to work. My guess is that it matched a very common pattern ("release on tag push") instead of reading the current trigger carefully.

This is exactly the kind of mistake that is easy to miss:

  • It sounds completely reasonable
  • It's in a well-formatted report next to six correct findings
  • It's only wrong in one detail

If I had just skimmed the report, I would have believed it.

Things I tested besides the reports

Bad input. I fed the CLI things a real user might get wrong: a folder that doesn't exist, a file instead of a folder, an unknown skill or agent name, a GitHub repo that doesn't exist. Every one gave a clear error, with no crash and no AI tokens wasted. I found two small issues (a negative --timeout was accepted, and an empty target quietly scanned the current folder) and reported them.

The dashboard. All pages loaded and the finding counts matched the reports, except the home page, which crashed with a 500 error. The cause was a recent change: agents that don't report cost now store "unknown" instead of $0, and the home page added the costs together with a plain sum(), which fails on an empty value. It was a one-line fix, and my PR for it (#31) is now merged.

What I learned

1. AI reviewers are genuinely useful. Most findings were correct, with the right file and line numbers. For coverage and speed, it's a huge help, especially for a small team.

2. "Looks professional" is not the same as "true". The one wrong detail was written just as confidently as the correct ones. Severity labels and neat tables don't make a finding correct.

3. Check against the right version of the code. Use the commit from the scan date. Otherwise you'll mark correct findings as wrong (or the other way round).

4. Keep a human in the loop for anything that matters. If a report is going to someone who will sign it off, every finding should be checked first. It took me a while, but it's much faster than reviewing the code from scratch.

Try it

Secfoo is free and open source (MIT). If you're a student or developer interested in security, try it on your own project and check the findings yourself. That's honestly the best way to learn what AI reviewers are good and bad at.

👉 https://github.com/secfoo-com/secfoo

Feedback, issues and contributions are welcome. I'd love to hear how it does on your code!

This is my second post about Secfoo. The first one was about catching an AI scanner inventing fake vulnerabilities.

security #ai #opensource #testing

title: H3 Martial-Arts and TaoMate Workflows: Read the Schedule, Not the Filename
summary: An eight-step filename is not an eight-step execution trace. Equally, a three-step scheduler can be genuinely configured without proving a particular speedup. These two H3 exports illustrate both distinctions. The package contains two JSON workflows: a martial-arts two-pass graph with 113 nodes and a TaoMate example collection with 239 nodes. Together they have 396 explicit links, plus named Set/Get relationships in the first file. This is a static walkthrough, not a new inference, audio review or hardware benchmark. The source title mentions 1080p and nearly one second per frame. Those remain source claims, not results measured for this guide. Export frame rate is not generation throughput. 01 — Resolve named inputs before counting references The martial-arts graph uses SetNode/GetNode pairs rather than direct visible wires for many inputs. Three image loaders are active: 159, 200 and 203. Their Set nodes publish IMAGE_0 , IMAGE_1 and IMAGE_2 ; the corresponding getters reach the first three reference-image slots of conditioner 136. Other image providers, all video providers and all source-audio providers are bypassed. Their getters can still be enabled and wired. Counting every visible getter would therefore overstate the active reference set. Check the compatible frontend's handling of named values and bypassed providers on import. The saved graph does not prove that every optional getter will resolve correctly in every installation. The prompt takes a similar route: active prompt node 194 feeds concatenation, then the live output of ShowText 297 feeds the named positive value and its getter. Extra prompt node 309 is bypassed. A cached ShowText string or the conditioner's old text is not an independent active prompt source. The scheduler receives 20, not the eight-step title PrimitiveInt 300 stores 20. It publishes the named value s , retrieved by node 401 and connected to BasicScheduler's steps input. That overrides the scheduler's saved local value of 10. The resulting sigma schedule passes through H3SigmaRefiner 361. Its named controls store extra_steps 1, start_at_sigma approximately 0.6, end_at_sigma 0 and cosine spacing. Both sampling stages receive the same refiner output. Do not turn this into a guessed 20+1 evaluation count: the custom refiner's implementation and sampler execution were not inspected or run. What the graph establishes is a linked 20-step input before transformation, not a verified eight-step run, an 8+8 split or a measured total NFE. The active Ref2V eight-step LoRA is a separate model selection. Its filename does not override that connected scheduler input. The alternative FL2V eight-step LoRA is bypassed. Read the model stack as a sequence The selected base is minimax_h3_hybrid_fl2va_ref2va_b25-49-bf16-v1.01.safetensors , with the selected INT8/ConvRot-named Qwen text encoder, FP16 video VAE and FP32 audio VAE. After the attention utilities and active Ref2V Turbo selection, Motion Repair is applied model-only at a linked strength of 0.2. The subsequent stack includes spatial-physics at model strength 0.3, wushu-e3 at 0.75, and another Motion Repair application at 0.5. Those final three LoraLoader nodes also store CLIP strength 1. The two Motion Repair applications should not be silently rewritten as one verified equivalent strength. Their positions and loader types differ. Likewise, attention and low-VRAM node names are not measured evidence of a particular kernel or memory reduction. The saved active media are images rather than a source motion-video sequence. This is reference conditioning plus model modifications and a prompt, not an explicit pose-map lock or proof of precise martial-arts motion transfer. The learned-upscale node does not promise a larger raster The coarse resolution selector requests 4:3, 1 megapixel and alignment to 32. Named width/height links override the conditioner's old 1344×768 values. The learned latent upscaler is also configured in megapixels mode targeting 1 MP , with alignment 32, CUDA, BF16 and chunking enabled. Its presence alone does not establish 2× enlargement, 1080p or a higher pixel count than the first stage. Inspect actual decoded dimensions. The duration control is 10 and feeds: max(5, round(a * 24)) + (5 - (max(5, round(a * 24)) % 17)) % 17 Arithmetic gives 243 requested frames, overriding the old 124-frame value. At configured 24 fps that is a nominal 10.125 seconds, not a measured output duration. Two sampling stages, two different first-stage outputs The first sampler's DENOISED_OUTPUT is split into video and audio latents. Only video passes through the learned upscaler; audio is carried into the concatenated second-stage latent. The second sampler reuses the same guider, positive conditioning and transformed sigma schedule. There is no separate rebuilt high-resolution conditioner in this graph. Carrying the audio latent forward does not prove that the final audio remains unchanged after another sampling stage. The first-stage save uses the first sampler's OUTPUT , not the DENOISED_OUTPUT sent toward upscaling. The second save uses the second sampler's OUTPUT . Each is routed into video and audio decoders, so this is not direct source-audio muxing. Both VHS save nodes use the prefix H3_Ref2VA二采 , despite belonging to different stages. Both store 24 fps, H.264, CRF 19 and trim_to_audio false. Identify the stage through connections, not that shared filename prefix. Compatibility of the audiovisual latent/decoder path and actual saved files still requires a test. 02 — Seven TaoMate examples are not seven working I2V runs The second JSON contains seven repeated branches. The letters below are audit labels, not authored project names or seven separately supplied workflow files. Branch Saved state What needs attention A Entire branch bypassed No active generation or save should be claimed from its stored controls B Main branch enabled, 9:16 Full selected LoRA stack with a connected first-frame image C Main branch enabled, 9:16 Similar stack, but not automatically a controlled comparison with B D Main branch enabled, 16:9 First-frame image loader is bypassed; do not label it assured I2V E Mixed enabled/bypassed nodes, 16:9 Save remains enabled while core generation/decoding is bypassed; inspect before queueing F Main branch enabled, 3:4 TaoMate and base wushu selections active; optional stack bypassed G Main branch enabled, 3:4 Newer wushu-action selection plus reference audio; Bunny selection bypassed An enabled SaveVideo node is not proof of a functioning upstream generation path. In particular, E needs review rather than being counted as a completed or successful example. Nor does static inspection alone certify that import will fail: verify the actual node/frontend behavior in a working copy. Three steps are configured, but speed is unmeasured Enabled main branches B, C, D, F and G use schedulers storing simple, 3 steps and denoise 1, with Euler selection. That three-step setting should not be dismissed merely because it has not been benchmarked. Their SelfLift controls store CFG 1, transition step 1, low-resolution scale 0.4, rho 0, weights 0.5–1 and the BF16 learned latent upscaler, with fixed seed control. These values do not prove actual intermediate dimensions, total model evaluations or latency. Extra seed-control widgets must not be mechanically zipped into named execution parameters. TaoMate's filename contains step3000 ; wushu filenames contain other step-like numbers. Those strings do not set inference steps. Model strengths come from linked PrimitiveFloat controls. The full B/C stack includes TaoMate 1, wushu 0.75, Combat and camera-motion at 0.35 each, spatial-physics 0.3, Motion Repair 0.2 and Bunny 0.1. D/F keep only TaoMate and the base wushu selection active. G substitutes the newer wushu-action file and leaves Bunny bypassed. These are different configurations and inputs, not a new matched speed or quality study. Dimensions and soundtrack still need separate checks All seven selectors store 1.4 MP and multiple 32, with the aspect ratios shown above. Connected dimensions override old local 1344×768 values. Do not promise fixed 1080p output from those controls. The linked duration expressions use the same nominal 10-to-243 arithmetic described earlier. CreateVideo stores 24 fps, 8-bit and sRGB controls; actual output dimensions, length and codec selection need inspection. An eight-step filename is not an eight-step execution trace. Equally, a three-step scheduler can be genuinely configured without proving a particular speedup. These two H3 exports illustrate both distinctions.

The package contains two JSON workflows: a martial-arts two-pass graph with 113 nodes and a TaoMate example collection with 239 nodes. Together they have 396 explicit links, plus named Set/Get relationships in the first file. This is a static walkthrough, not a new inference, audio review or hardware benchmark.

The source title mentions 1080p and nearly one second per frame. Those remain source claims, not results measured for this guide. Export frame rate is not generation throughput.

01 — Resolve named inputs before counting references

The martial-arts graph uses SetNode/GetNode pairs rather than direct visible wires for many inputs. Three image loaders are active: 159, 200 and 203. Their Set nodes publish IMAGE_0, IMAGE_1 and IMAGE_2; the corresponding getters reach the first three reference-image slots of conditioner 136.

Other image providers, all video providers and all source-audio providers are bypassed. Their getters can still be enabled and wired. Counting every visible getter would therefore overstate the active reference set.

Check the compatible frontend's handling of named values and bypassed providers on import. The saved graph does not prove that every optional getter will resolve correctly in every installation.

The prompt takes a similar route: active prompt node 194 feeds concatenation, then the live output of ShowText 297 feeds the named positive value and its getter. Extra prompt node 309 is bypassed. A cached ShowText string or the conditioner's old text is not an independent active prompt source.

The scheduler receives 20, not the eight-step title

PrimitiveInt 300 stores 20. It publishes the named value s, retrieved by node 401 and connected to BasicScheduler's steps input. That overrides the scheduler's saved local value of 10.

The resulting sigma schedule passes through H3SigmaRefiner 361. Its named controls store extra_steps 1, start_at_sigma approximately 0.6, end_at_sigma 0 and cosine spacing. Both sampling stages receive the same refiner output.

Do not turn this into a guessed 20+1 evaluation count: the custom refiner's implementation and sampler execution were not inspected or run. What the graph establishes is a linked 20-step input before transformation, not a verified eight-step run, an 8+8 split or a measured total NFE.

The active Ref2V eight-step LoRA is a separate model selection. Its filename does not override that connected scheduler input. The alternative FL2V eight-step LoRA is bypassed.

Read the model stack as a sequence

The selected base is minimax_h3_hybrid_fl2va_ref2va_b25-49-bf16-v1.01.safetensors, with the selected INT8/ConvRot-named Qwen text encoder, FP16 video VAE and FP32 audio VAE.

After the attention utilities and active Ref2V Turbo selection, Motion Repair is applied model-only at a linked strength of 0.2. The subsequent stack includes spatial-physics at model strength 0.3, wushu-e3 at 0.75, and another Motion Repair application at 0.5. Those final three LoraLoader nodes also store CLIP strength 1.

The two Motion Repair applications should not be silently rewritten as one verified equivalent strength. Their positions and loader types differ. Likewise, attention and low-VRAM node names are not measured evidence of a particular kernel or memory reduction.

The saved active media are images rather than a source motion-video sequence. This is reference conditioning plus model modifications and a prompt, not an explicit pose-map lock or proof of precise martial-arts motion transfer.

The learned-upscale node does not promise a larger raster

The coarse resolution selector requests 4:3, 1 megapixel and alignment to 32. Named width/height links override the conditioner's old 1344×768 values.

The learned latent upscaler is also configured in megapixels mode targeting 1 MP, with alignment 32, CUDA, BF16 and chunking enabled. Its presence alone does not establish 2× enlargement, 1080p or a higher pixel count than the first stage. Inspect actual decoded dimensions.

The duration control is 10 and feeds:

max(5, round(a * 24))
+ (5 - (max(5, round(a * 24)) % 17)) % 17

Arithmetic gives 243 requested frames, overriding the old 124-frame value. At configured 24 fps that is a nominal 10.125 seconds, not a measured output duration.

Two sampling stages, two different first-stage outputs

The first sampler's DENOISED_OUTPUT is split into video and audio latents. Only video passes through the learned upscaler; audio is carried into the concatenated second-stage latent.

The second sampler reuses the same guider, positive conditioning and transformed sigma schedule. There is no separate rebuilt high-resolution conditioner in this graph. Carrying the audio latent forward does not prove that the final audio remains unchanged after another sampling stage.

The first-stage save uses the first sampler's OUTPUT, not the DENOISED_OUTPUT sent toward upscaling. The second save uses the second sampler's OUTPUT. Each is routed into video and audio decoders, so this is not direct source-audio muxing.

Both VHS save nodes use the prefix H3_Ref2VA二采, despite belonging to different stages. Both store 24 fps, H.264, CRF 19 and trim_to_audio false. Identify the stage through connections, not that shared filename prefix. Compatibility of the audiovisual latent/decoder path and actual saved files still requires a test.

02 — Seven TaoMate examples are not seven working I2V runs

The second JSON contains seven repeated branches. The letters below are audit labels, not authored project names or seven separately supplied workflow files.

Branch Saved state What needs attention A Entire branch bypassed No active generation or save should be claimed from its stored controls B Main branch enabled, 9:16 Full selected LoRA stack with a connected first-frame image C Main branch enabled, 9:16 Similar stack, but not automatically a controlled comparison with B D Main branch enabled, 16:9 First-frame image loader is bypassed; do not label it assured I2V E Mixed enabled/bypassed nodes, 16:9 Save remains enabled while core generation/decoding is bypassed; inspect before queueing F Main branch enabled, 3:4 TaoMate and base wushu selections active; optional stack bypassed G Main branch enabled, 3:4 Newer wushu-action selection plus reference audio; Bunny selection bypassed

An enabled SaveVideo node is not proof of a functioning upstream generation path. In particular, E needs review rather than being counted as a completed or successful example. Nor does static inspection alone certify that import will fail: verify the actual node/frontend behavior in a working copy.

Three steps are configured, but speed is unmeasured

Enabled main branches B, C, D, F and G use schedulers storing simple, 3 steps and denoise 1, with Euler selection. That three-step setting should not be dismissed merely because it has not been benchmarked.

Their SelfLift controls store CFG 1, transition step 1, low-resolution scale 0.4, rho 0, weights 0.5–1 and the BF16 learned latent upscaler, with fixed seed control. These values do not prove actual intermediate dimensions, total model evaluations or latency. Extra seed-control widgets must not be mechanically zipped into named execution parameters.

TaoMate's filename contains step3000; wushu filenames contain other step-like numbers. Those strings do not set inference steps.

Model strengths come from linked PrimitiveFloat controls. The full B/C stack includes TaoMate 1, wushu 0.75, Combat and camera-motion at 0.35 each, spatial-physics 0.3, Motion Repair 0.2 and Bunny 0.1. D/F keep only TaoMate and the base wushu selection active. G substitutes the newer wushu-action file and leaves Bunny bypassed.

These are different configurations and inputs, not a new matched speed or quality study.

Dimensions and soundtrack still need separate checks

All seven selectors store 1.4 MP and multiple 32, with the aspect ratios shown above. Connected dimensions override old local 1344×768 values. Do not promise fixed 1080p output from those controls.

Only G has a loaded audio connection, and it enters the reference-audio conditioning port. It is not drive_audio, final_audio or a direct soundtrack connection. All CreateVideo audio inputs come from sampled-audio decoders.

That distinction matters for voice or lip-sync requirements. An audio reference does not prove the original waveform is preserved, the same spoken content is reproduced, or the output lips align correctly. Listen to the result rather than treating the input connection as acceptance evidence.

title: Let your LLM say I don't know instead of guessing
summary: Your user asks a factual question. The model returns a polished paragraph. Nothing in the stack threw an error. That is exactly when you are most exposed. A language model generates the most plausible next words, not the most true ones, so a wrong answer can look identical to a right one. That mechanism is what people call AI hallucination : same token prediction, missing or weak facts, fluent fiction at the end. Dan Klein , co-founder and CTO of Scaled Cognition, put the internals this way on Chain of Thought: we label outputs after the fact, but the model never splits “truth” from “guess” on its own. If they're right, we call them truth. And if they're wrong, we call them hallucination. But the model does not internally distinguish between those. Dan Klein, co-founder and CTO of Scaled Cognition I’d stop treating confidence in the UI as a proxy for correctness. Treat every fluent sentence as a claim you still owe evidence for. Why does fluency hide the errors you care about? Obvious mistakes get caught in QA. Klein’s audit story from enterprise work is worse: when his team audits enterprise systems, he says, the real hallucination rate is often about five times what the customer has noticed, because the rest are fluent enough to pass. His examples are a refund policy that is real and plausible but not yours, or yours but for a customer with a different status. Looks right. It looks right and is right are not the same. It is very hard to detect hallucinations when they are packaged up sufficiently fluently. Dan Klein, co-founder and CTO of Scaled Cognition Chip Huyen made the data angle plain on Chain of Thought ep 5: missing or wrong context pushes the model toward invention. Models are more likely to hallucinate when it does not have access to the necessary and correct information to answer questions. Chip Huyen, author of AI Engineering So the design job is to give the model the facts at answer time, allow silence when facts are missing, and verify what still matters. A smarter model does not remove that work. What breaks when you only punish wrong guesses? Pre-training shows the model fluent text, not labeled false statements. Rare facts (like a specific birthday) do not repeat as patterns, so the model still produces something that sounds like an answer. Benchmarks make the incentive worse: “I don’t know” often scores like a wrong answer, while a random guess sometimes hits. OpenAI’s 2025 write-up on why language models hallucinate argues for penalizing confident errors more than honest uncertainty. Anthropic’s interpretability work on Claude describes a default to decline on unrecognized entities, with a “known entity” signal that can flip that off and invite a guess anyway. For your app, that means instructions that forbid uncertainty fight the same scoreboards that trained the model to guess. If your eval sheet marks abstain as a miss, you are training your team to ship guessers. How do you ground answers and still leave an out? Grounding means building the reply from material you put in context at question time, ideally with citations per claim. That cuts invented detail because the model has less room to freestyle. It does not guarantee truth: sources can be stale, retrieval can miss the doc, and the model can still stretch past what the sources say. Many production issues that look like “model bugs” are retrieval or document problems first. General models also carry a knowledge cutoff : training frozen at a date, then released later. Ask about anything newer and you get “I don’t know” or a plausible guess. The standard fix is the same as grounding: fetch current or private text into the context window before generation (RAG, search, or both). My default pattern for factual features: Retrieve candidate passages for the question. If nothing passes a relevance threshold, return abstain (or escalate to a human). Do not ask the model to “try anyway.” If you have passages, instruct answer-only-from-these, cite span or doc id per claim. Run a faithfulness check on answers that can move money, policy, or compliance. Step 4 is where AI evaluation and reliability work pays off: separate counts for answered , abstained , answered_supported and answered_unsupported . What does an abstain-and-ground sketch look like? Label this as illustration, not production code from any guest or vendor. # Sketch: abstain if retrieval is weak; answer only from chunks MIN_SCORE = 0.42 # tune on your corpus def answer ( user_question : str , retrieve , llm , faithfulness_check ): chunks = retrieve ( user_question , top_k = 8 ) best = max (( c . score for c in chunks ), default = 0.0 ) if best < MIN_SCORE : return { " status " : " abstain " , " message " : " No trusted source found. " } prompt = { " instruction " : ( " Answer using ONLY the sources. " " If they do not support an answer, reply ABSTAIN. " ), " sources " : [ c . text for c in chunks ], " question " : user_question , } draft = llm . complete ( prompt ) if " ABSTAIN " in draft : return { " status " : " abstain " , " message " : " Model declined. " } if not faithfulness_check ( draft , chunks ): return { " status " : " abstain " , " message " : " Failed source check. " } return { " status " : " ok " , " text " : draft , " sources " : chunks } The abstain path is a first-class HTTP response, not a thrown exception buried in logs. Users should see “we don’t know” when you mean it. Checklist Decide where a wrong fluent answer is costly; tighten grounding and checks there first. Retrieve before generate; abstain when retrieval is empty or weak instead of prompting harder. Tell the model abstaining is allowed; score abstain better than a confident wrong answer in evals. Check high-stakes outputs against supplied sources (faithfulness), not vibes. Remember fluent output is plausible text until your sources and checks say otherwise. The longer explainer, with the episode clips, is on Chain of Thought . It draws on this episode . Subscribe to the Chain of Thought newsletter for new episodes and write-ups like this one. summary_html:
Your user asks a factual question. The model returns a polished paragraph. Nothing in the stack threw an error. That is exactly when you are most exposed. A language model generates the most plausible next words, not the most true ones, so a wrong answer can look identical to a right one. That mechanism is what people call AI hallucination: same token prediction, missing or weak facts, fluent fiction at the end.

Dan Klein, co-founder and CTO of Scaled Cognition, put the internals this way on Chain of Thought: we label outputs after the fact, but the model never splits “truth” from “guess” on its own.

If they're right, we call them truth. And if they're wrong, we call them hallucination. But the model does not internally distinguish between those.

Dan Klein, co-founder and CTO of Scaled Cognition

I’d stop treating confidence in the UI as a proxy for correctness. Treat every fluent sentence as a claim you still owe evidence for.

Why does fluency hide the errors you care about?

Obvious mistakes get caught in QA. Klein’s audit story from enterprise work is worse: when his team audits enterprise systems, he says, the real hallucination rate is often about five times what the customer has noticed, because the rest are fluent enough to pass. His examples are a refund policy that is real and plausible but not yours, or yours but for a customer with a different status.

Looks right. It looks right and is right are not the same. It is very hard to detect hallucinations when they are packaged up sufficiently fluently.

Dan Klein, co-founder and CTO of Scaled Cognition

Chip Huyen made the data angle plain on Chain of Thought ep 5: missing or wrong context pushes the model toward invention.

Models are more likely to hallucinate when it does not have access to the necessary and correct information to answer questions.

Chip Huyen, author of AI Engineering

So the design job is to give the model the facts at answer time, allow silence when facts are missing, and verify what still matters. A smarter model does not remove that work.

What breaks when you only punish wrong guesses?

Pre-training shows the model fluent text, not labeled false statements. Rare facts (like a specific birthday) do not repeat as patterns, so the model still produces something that sounds like an answer. Benchmarks make the incentive worse: “I don’t know” often scores like a wrong answer, while a random guess sometimes hits. OpenAI’s 2025 write-up on why language models hallucinate argues for penalizing confident errors more than honest uncertainty. Anthropic’s interpretability work on Claude describes a default to decline on unrecognized entities, with a “known entity” signal that can flip that off and invite a guess anyway.

For your app, that means instructions that forbid uncertainty fight the same scoreboards that trained the model to guess. If your eval sheet marks abstain as a miss, you are training your team to ship guessers.

How do you ground answers and still leave an out?

Grounding means building the reply from material you put in context at question time, ideally with citations per claim. That cuts invented detail because the model has less room to freestyle. It does not guarantee truth: sources can be stale, retrieval can miss the doc, and the model can still stretch past what the sources say. Many production issues that look like “model bugs” are retrieval or document problems first.

General models also carry a knowledge cutoff: training frozen at a date, then released later. Ask about anything newer and you get “I don’t know” or a plausible guess. The standard fix is the same as grounding: fetch current or private text into the context window before generation (RAG, search, or both).

My default pattern for factual features:

  1. Retrieve candidate passages for the question.
  2. If nothing passes a relevance threshold, return abstain (or escalate to a human). Do not ask the model to “try anyway.”
  3. If you have passages, instruct answer-only-from-these, cite span or doc id per claim.
  4. Run a faithfulness check on answers that can move money, policy, or compliance.

Step 4 is where AI evaluation and reliability work pays off: separate counts for answered, abstained, answered_supported and answered_unsupported.

What does an abstain-and-ground sketch look like?

Label this as illustration, not production code from any guest or vendor.

# Sketch: abstain if retrieval is weak; answer only from chunks

MIN_SCORE = 0.42  # tune on your corpus

def answer(user_question: str, retrieve, llm, faithfulness_check):
    chunks = retrieve(user_question, top_k=8)
    best = max((c.score for c in chunks), default=0.0)
    if best < MIN_SCORE:
        return {"status": "abstain", "message": "No trusted source found."}

    prompt = {
        "instruction": (
            "Answer using ONLY the sources. "
            "If they do not support an answer, reply ABSTAIN."
        ),
        "sources": [c.text for c in chunks],
        "question": user_question,
    }
    draft = llm.complete(prompt)
    if "ABSTAIN" in draft:
        return {"status": "abstain", "message": "Model declined."}

    if not faithfulness_check(draft, chunks):
        return {"status": "abstain", "message": "Failed source check."}

    return {"status": "ok", "text": draft, "sources": chunks}

The abstain path is a first-class HTTP response, not a thrown exception buried in logs. Users should see “we don’t know” when you mean it.

Checklist
  • Decide where a wrong fluent answer is costly; tighten grounding and checks there first.
  • Retrieve before generate; abstain when retrieval is empty or weak instead of prompting harder.
  • Tell the model abstaining is allowed; score abstain better than a confident wrong answer in evals.
  • Check high-stakes outputs against supplied sources (faithfulness), not vibes.
  • Remember fluent output is plausible text until your sources and checks say otherwise.
