title: Best WordPress Multilingual Plugins for 2027: Workflow, Cost and Control
summary: Originally published on LumoWP . Choosing a multilingual plugin is easy when the demo contains one paragraph and a language switcher. The difficult part comes later: a translated product goes out of stock, an Elementor template changes, a subscription renews, or an editor rewrites a sentence that already has five translations. That is where this comparison starts. The best WordPress multilingual plugin for your site is the one whose workflow still makes sense after the first translation. About this 2027 guide Researched on October 31, 2026 for people planning a 2027 website. Features and prices below describe the documentation available on that date, not unreleased 2027 versions. This is a documented workflow comparison, not a five-plugin performance benchmark. LumoWP sells a WPML AI translation add-on; that relationship is disclosed where it appears. The shortlist: which plugin fits which job? There is no useful universal winner. Start with the part of your website that would be hardest to translate and maintain—not the easiest page in the demo. Plugin A strong starting point for Main working model The decision you must accept WPML Editorial teams, complex WordPress content and multilingual WooCommerce Connected language versions with translation jobs and integrations Configure the right components and test your actual builder widgets Polylang A manually maintained bilingual site or a WordPress-native editorial workflow Language assignments and relationships between content Budget separately for advanced workflows and WooCommerce TranslatePress Owners who want to translate while looking at the front end Translate rendered strings through a visual editor Plan for SEO features, source-text changes and dynamic states Weglot Teams that prefer a managed translation service and a quick operational start WordPress integration with a hosted translation service Ongoing service cost, language limits and total translated-word allowance MultilingualPress Separate regional sites with their own teams and store settings One language site per WordPress Multisite network site Network administration is part of the project These are recommendations by use case, not measured rankings. A simple two-language brochure site and a store with subscriptions, custom product fields and regional pricing should not receive the same recommendation. First understand what the plugin actually translates Think of a multilingual website as four connected systems: content storage, translation production, public URLs, and ongoing maintenance. A plugin may make the second part easy while asking you to do more work in the fourth. With a content-based workflow, an editor works with related language versions. With a rendered-string workflow, the translation layer works with text that appears on the page. With a multisite workflow, each language has its own site. A hosted service adds another question: what happens to the public translated experience if the subscription stops? None of these models is automatically faster, more professional or better for Google. They create different operational responsibilities. Your checkout, search results, logged-in dashboard and reusable templates are more informative test cases than a static About page. Conceptual illustration, not a software screenshot. WPML: a strong candidate for structured content and complex stores WPML is worth shortlisting when translation is an ongoing editorial process rather than a one-time conversion. Its Multilingual CMS and Agency plans include the advanced translation workflow and integrations needed for more involved sites. The cheaper Blog plan is a different scope, not simply the same product with fewer site licenses. Check the current WPML plan comparison before choosing it for a builder-heavy site. For Elementor, start with the official integration instructions . Translate reusable templates as well as pages. A translated page can still display a source-language header if the header comes from a separate template. Custom widgets can also need field registration; a page-builder compatibility badge does not tell you whether every third-party widget in your project exposes its fields correctly. My decision rule: shortlist WPML when you need a coordinated translation workflow across posts, products, taxonomies and templates. Before committing, include your most unusual widget and your most complicated product in the pilot. For an existing site, do not buy another translation tool just because an update is missing. Our WPML and Elementor troubleshooting guide explains how to separate a missing field, a template issue and an outdated translation before translating again. What to check before paying for automatic translation The plugin license and translation usage are different cost items. WPML's current automatic translation pricing documentation describes AI-word billing and different handling of edits depending on the workflow. Do not copy a calculation from an older article about credits and assume it still applies to your selected engine and account. Ask a practical question: if your team updates fifty product descriptions every week, what gets sent again, what is reused, and where can you inspect the charge? Calculate that before enabling a large automatic job. Conceptual illustration, not a software screenshot. Polylang: attractive when editors want direct control Polylang is a sensible starting point for a site with a manageable number of languages and editors who can maintain the translated content. Its free version covers core multilingual content, while Pro adds workflow features such as duplication and expanded slug handling. WooCommerce has its own paid integration. The official feature matrix makes these boundaries clearer than a generic “free versus paid” label. An easy setup mistake is leaving existing content without a language assignment. Follow the setup wizard guidance and check existing posts, pages and navigation after assigning the default language. My decision rule: choose Polylang for editorial control, not because somebody promises that fewer features must mean better performance. Compare the complete stack you actually need, including the WooCommerce add-on where relevant. The Elementor and automatic-translation detail that matters Polylang Pro offers DeepL translation using your own API connection, but its current pricing matrix explicitly says this machine-translation feature is not compatible with Elementor. That is a limitation of this specific workflow, not a claim that no Polylang-and-Elementor site can exist. If your brief says “automatically translate all Elementor pages,” resolve that requirement before choosing a plan. For a closer comparison of the editorial models, see Polylang versus WPML . Conceptual illustration, not a software screenshot. TranslatePress: useful when translation starts with what visitors see TranslatePress takes a visual approach: work with the front end and translate the text in context. This can be easier for an owner who recognizes a button on the page but does not know which plugin generated it. The important technical detail is persistence. Its automatic translation documentation explains that generated translations are stored in the database rather than requested from the translation API on every page view. That does not mean the complete site has zero translation-related runtime cost; it means repeated API generation is not the normal delivery model. My decision rule: shortlist it when visual editing suits your team and your important front-end states can be reproduced for translation and review. Test a validation error, a cart update and an account page—not only visible text on the initial page load. Source edits need a maintenance plan TranslatePress's FAQ describes the distinction between an original string and its translation. Changing the source can create a new string to translate, while the old translation remains stored. That is different from an editor thinking “I changed one paragraph in this translated post.” Try this before rollout: translate a page, change its heading and one repeated call-to-action in the source, then inspect the translated page. Write down what needs review. This small experiment tells your editorial team more than a screenshot of the translation sidebar. Conceptual illustration, not a software screenshot. Weglot: a service decision as much as a plugin decision Weglot is appealing when the team wants to manage translation through a hosted service. The trade-off is a recurring service relationship with word and language allowances. One pricing detail deserves attention: the Weglot pricing page describes a total translated-word allowance across the project, not a fresh allowance that resets every month. If a simplified 20,000-word source corpus is translated into three languages, use roughly 60,000 translated words as an initial planning estimate, then verify the actual counted content. Navigation, dynamic text and the service's counting rules can change the result. My decision rule: shortlist Weglot when the ongoing service model is acceptable and the team values that workflow. Compare the plan required for your whole translated corpus, not just the starting price. Cancellation is an operational requirement Weglot's cancellation documentation says translated content stops appearing when the relevant paid service is cancelled or paused. Treat exit planning as part of selection. Ask what you can export, what URLs you would need to preserve, and how you would replace the translated delivery layer before cancelling. This is not the same question as whether you retain a copy of translated text. Owning an export and continuing to serve the same multilingual website are two different things. Conceptual illustration, not a software screenshot. MultilingualPress: when markets need separate sites MultilingualPress uses WordPress Multisite, with each language on its own site. Its documentation presents independent content and configuration as central to the design. That makes it interesting when your German and French operations need more independence than translated paragraphs: different teams, different catalogs or different site settings. It also means backups, network permissions, deployment and integrations must be planned for a network. My decision rule: shortlist it when separate sites are an intentional business requirement. Do not convert a simple brochure site to Multisite merely because a comparison labels the architecture “enterprise.” A useful question for the agency is: who owns the relationship between the sites after launch? If nobody will maintain cross-language links and shared requirements, architectural independence can turn into editorial drift. What about GTranslate and Loco Translate? GTranslate belongs in the discussion, but distinguish its free translation widget from its paid multilingual SEO offering. The WordPress.org listing lists indexable language URLs and related SEO features in the paid offering. Choosing a multilingual plugin is easy when the demo contains one paragraph and a language switcher. The difficult part comes later: a translated product goes out of stock, an Elementor template changes, a subscription renews, or an editor rewrites a sentence that already has five translations.

That is where this comparison starts. The best WordPress multilingual plugin for your site is the one whose workflow still makes sense after the first translation.

About this 2027 guide
Researched on October 31, 2026 for people planning a 2027 website. Features and prices below describe the documentation available on that date, not unreleased 2027 versions. This is a documented workflow comparison, not a five-plugin performance benchmark. LumoWP sells a WPML AI translation add-on; that relationship is disclosed where it appears.

The shortlist: which plugin fits which job?

There is no useful universal winner. Start with the part of your website that would be hardest to translate and maintain—not the easiest page in the demo.

These are recommendations by use case, not measured rankings. A simple two-language brochure site and a store with subscriptions, custom product fields and regional pricing should not receive the same recommendation.

First understand what the plugin actually translates

Think of a multilingual website as four connected systems: content storage, translation production, public URLs, and ongoing maintenance. A plugin may make the second part easy while asking you to do more work in the fourth.

With a content-based workflow, an editor works with related language versions. With a rendered-string workflow, the translation layer works with text that appears on the page. With a multisite workflow, each language has its own site. A hosted service adds another question: what happens to the public translated experience if the subscription stops?

None of these models is automatically faster, more professional or better for Google. They create different operational responsibilities. Your checkout, search results, logged-in dashboard and reusable templates are more informative test cases than a static About page.

Conceptual illustration, not a software screenshot.

WPML is worth shortlisting when translation is an ongoing editorial process rather than a one-time conversion. Its Multilingual CMS and Agency plans include the advanced translation workflow and integrations needed for more involved sites. The cheaper Blog plan is a different scope, not simply the same product with fewer site licenses. Check the current WPML plan comparison before choosing it for a builder-heavy site.

For Elementor, start with the official integration instructions. Translate reusable templates as well as pages. A translated page can still display a source-language header if the header comes from a separate template. Custom widgets can also need field registration; a page-builder compatibility badge does not tell you whether every third-party widget in your project exposes its fields correctly.

My decision rule: shortlist WPML when you need a coordinated translation workflow across posts, products, taxonomies and templates. Before committing, include your most unusual widget and your most complicated product in the pilot.

For an existing site, do not buy another translation tool just because an update is missing. Our WPML and Elementor troubleshooting guide explains how to separate a missing field, a template issue and an outdated translation before translating again.

What to check before paying for automatic translation

The plugin license and translation usage are different cost items. WPML's current automatic translation pricing documentation describes AI-word billing and different handling of edits depending on the workflow. Do not copy a calculation from an older article about credits and assume it still applies to your selected engine and account.

Ask a practical question: if your team updates fifty product descriptions every week, what gets sent again, what is reused, and where can you inspect the charge? Calculate that before enabling a large automatic job.

Polylang is a sensible starting point for a site with a manageable number of languages and editors who can maintain the translated content. Its free version covers core multilingual content, while Pro adds workflow features such as duplication and expanded slug handling. WooCommerce has its own paid integration. Polylang Pro offers DeepL translation using your own API connection, but its current pricing matrix explicitly says this machine-translation feature is not compatible with Elementor. That is a limitation of this specific workflow, not a claim that no Polylang-and-Elementor site can exist.

If your brief says “automatically translate all Elementor pages,” resolve that requirement before choosing a plan. For a closer comparison of the editorial models, see Polylang versus WPML.

TranslatePress takes a visual approach: work with the front end and translate the text in context. This can be easier for an owner who recognizes a button on the page but does not know which plugin generated it.

Its automatic translation documentation explains that generated translations are stored in the database rather than requested from the translation API on every page view. That does not mean the complete site has zero translation-related runtime cost; it means repeated API generation is not the normal delivery model.

My decision rule: shortlist it when visual editing suits your team and your important front-end states can be reproduced for translation and review. Test a validation error, a cart update and an account page—not only visible text on the initial page load.

TranslatePress's FAQ describes the distinction between an original string and its translation. Changing the source can create a new string to translate, while the old translation remains stored. That is different from an editor thinking “I changed one paragraph in this translated post.”

Try this before rollout: translate a page, change its heading and one repeated call-to-action in the source, then inspect the translated page. Write down what needs review. This small experiment tells your editorial team more than a screenshot of the translation sidebar.

Weglot is appealing when the team wants to manage translation through a hosted service. The trade-off is a recurring service relationship with word and language allowances.

My decision rule: shortlist Weglot when the ongoing service model is acceptable and the team values that workflow. Compare the plan required for your whole translated corpus, not just the starting price.

Weglot's cancellation documentation says translated content stops appearing when the relevant paid service is cancelled or paused. Treat exit planning as part of selection. This is not the same question as whether you retain a copy of translated text. Owning an export and continuing to serve the same multilingual website are two different things.

Conceptual illustration, not a software screenshot.

MultilingualPress uses WordPress Multisite, with each language on its own site. Its documentation presents independent content and configuration as central to the design.

My decision rule: shortlist it when separate sites are an intentional business requirement. Do not convert a simple brochure site to Multisite merely because a comparison labels the architecture “enterprise.”

A useful question for the agency is: who owns the relationship between the sites after launch? If nobody will maintain cross-language links and shared requirements, architectural independence can turn into editorial drift.

Whether you’re building a smart assistant, a game NPC, or a podcast generator, the core building blocks—speech recognition, synthesis, and cloning—are now accessible through open APIs and cloud services. In this post we’ll walk through the fundamentals, show you how to hit the ground running with a quick Python/TTS demo, and explain why ElevenLabs is a top‑choice for high‑quality voice synthesis. 1. The Voice AI Landscape Layer What it does Typical APIs Speech Recognition (STT) Converts spoken audio into text. Amazon Polly, Google Cloud TTS, ElevenLabs Voice Cloning / Voice Conversion Re‑creates a specific speaker’s voice or adapts a voice model. Respeecher, Descript’s Overdub, ElevenLabs The synergy of these layers lets you build full‑fledged conversational agents: User speaks → STT → NLP → TTS → Speaker hears . The key to a smooth experience is low latency, high fidelity, and a voice that feels natural. 2. Why Text‑to‑Speech Matters You might think that speech recognition is the hard part, but TTS has become equally critical. A robotic or garbled voice can ruin user experience. Modern TTS engines use neural networks (e.g., Tacotron, FastSpeech) that generate waveforms with human‑like prosody, pauses, and emotion.     "Content-Type": "application/json"
}

# 3️⃣ Call the API

    f"{BASE_URL}/text-to-speech/{voice_id}",
    headers=headers,
    json=payload,
    stream=True
)

# 4️⃣ Save the streamed audio to a file
with open("output.mp3", "wb") as f:
    for chunk in response.iter_content(chunk_size=8192):
        if chunk:
            f.write(chunk)

print("✅ Audio saved to output.mp3")

The same concept works in JavaScript or via a curl call, so pick whichever stack feels natural to you.

4. Voice Cloning: Re‑creating a Speaker

Voice cloning lets you synthesize speech that sounds like a specific person. The process typically involves:

  1. Collecting a clean recording of the target speaker (30‑60 seconds is enough for many services).
  2. Uploading the audio and letting the model learn the speaker’s timbre, cadence, and pronunciation.
  3. Generating new utterances using the cloned voice.

ElevenLabs offers a straightforward API for cloning, and the quality is comparable to the best commercial services. The only downside is the amount of data needed for a truly natural clone—generally a few minutes of speech.

5. Building a Simple Voice Assistant

Let’s put it all together: a minimal assistant that listens to a user, transcribes the speech, processes a simple command, and replies using TTS. We’ll use Python with the speech_recognition library for STT and the ElevenLabs API for TTS.

import speech_recognition as sr
import requests
import json

API_KEY = "YOUR_ELEVENLABS_API_KEY"
BASE_URL = "https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1"

def synthesize(text, voice="Bella"):
    payload = {
        "text": text,
        "voice_settings": {
            "stability": 0.6,
            "similarity_boost": 0.5
        }
    }
    headers = {
        "xi-api-key": API_KEY,
        "Content-Type": "application/json"
    }
    resp = requests.post(
        f"{BASE_URL}/text-to-speech/{voice}",
        headers=headers,
        json=payload,
        stream=True
    )
    with open("response.mp3", "wb") as f:
        for chunk in resp.iter_content(chunk_size=8192):
            f.write(chunk)
    print("✅ TTS completed. Playing audio...")

def main():
    r = sr.Recognizer()
    with sr.Microphone() as source:
        print("🎙️  Listening…")
        audio = r.listen(source)

    try:
        user_text = r.recognize_google(audio)
        print(f"You said: {user_text}")
        # Simple command: if user says "time", reply with current time
        if "time" in user_text.lower():
            from datetime import datetime
            reply = f"The time is {datetime.now().strftime('%I:%M %p')}."
        else:
            reply = "Sorry, I didn’t get that."
        synthesize(reply)
    except sr.UnknownValueError:
        print("❌ Could not understand audio.")
    except sr.RequestError as e:
        print(f"❌ Could not request results; {e}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

What you’ll learn from this snippet:

  • How to capture microphone input in real time.
  • Basic STT with Google’s free API (you can swap out any other STT provider).
  • A clean separation between recognition, logic, and synthesis.
  • Easy integration with ElevenLabs for high‑quality speech output.
6. Tips for Production‑Ready Voice AI
Concern Recommendation Latency Use streaming TTS endpoints; cache short phrases. Privacy Keep user audio on-device or encrypt before sending. Scalability Use a CDN for static voice assets; consider serverless functions for on‑the‑fly synthesis. Cost Monitor API usage; many providers offer tiered pricing with free quotas.

If you’re serious about building a voice product, start by profiling your application’s bottlenecks. Even a 200 ms latency can feel laggy for a conversational agent.

7. Wrap‑Up

Voice AI is no longer a niche research area—it’s a developer playground. By combining open‑source STT models with powerful TTS services like ElevenLabs, you can create rich, interactive audio experiences in a matter of days. Whether you’re prototyping a chatbot, generating audiobooks, or cloning a celebrity voice for a marketing campaign, the tools are ready and the learning curve is gentle.

title: 10Eros Beta5 in H3: Two-Pass Refinement Versus SelfLift Audio Conditioning
summary: These two exports use the same selected Beta5 base-model filename, but they are not interchangeable presets. One builds a coarse-to-refined audiovisual result from active image references. The other manually injects trimmed source audio into an audiovisual latent and uses a SelfLift sampler. The differences matter before you queue either graph: which inputs are active, which schedule reaches the sampler, where output audio comes from, and which branches actually save files. The supplied files contain 66 and 32 nodes respectively, totaling 98 nodes and 155 links. Their visible nodes and connected wires do not establish active media inputs. The conditioners request AUTO/native behavior, so do not describe this saved state as an active first/last-frame or source-audio-driven example simply because the filename mentions those modes. Reference slots are sparse. Check how the matching custom implementation resolves prompt Picture ordinals rather than assuming a slot suffix is a direct picture-number guarantee. Follow the linked prompt and dimensions Prompt node 28 supplies the active instruction. The older red-Hanfu text stored inside the conditioners is overridden. Refinement adds a separate sharpness/natural-photorealism instruction through concatenation. That is another requested behavior, not proof that skin, faces or texture improve without changing identity. The coarse resolution selector stores 4:3, 1 megapixel, multiple 32 . Its links override the conditioner's old 736×416 values. The learned latent upscaler is configured as scale_by 1.5, and its width/height outputs feed the second conditioner. Stored 1344×768 and upscaler target-size fields do not define the effective output size in this route. Inspect actual dimensions after execution rather than quoting those defaults. The active LoRA stacks differ between stages The selected base is 10Eros_Max_h3_TURBO-hybrid_beta5_int8_SinoX.safetensors . The FL2VA Turbo LoRA at node 5 is bypassed. Both ExposureSlider nodes are also bypassed, despite retained strengths. The coarse stack applies Combat at 0.7, the aesthetic and FrameRush selections at 0.5 each, and Motion Repair at 0.7. The refinement stack uses Combat at 0.49, the same aesthetic/FrameRush strengths, Motion Repair at 0.2, and an additional LMS selection at 0.3. These are configured selections, not verified effects. The “small-face” or “de-oiling” label does not make this a dedicated face-detection/crop/stitch graph. It uses a broader learned-latent two-pass route; there is no separate face-crop repair chain in this export. Attention-related patches are enabled upstream. Their names do not independently establish the effective runtime kernel, VRAM savings, compatible hardware or acceleration. Resolve the installed implementations before relying on their interactions. The connected schedule is not the old eight-step sigma output DualClockSampler node 8 stores a steps value of 8 and supplies model/sampler outputs, but its SIGMAS output is unconnected . LearnedTwoPassParityPlan node 9 supplies the connected schedules, with saved base/coarse/refine controls of 9 / 4 / 5 . Follow those connections rather than advertising an eight-step coarse run. Nor should the planned 4+5 split be presented as a measured total number of model evaluations: diagnostics are unused and the custom samplers/mixer were not executed here. The first sampler's DENOISED_OUTPUT reaches the learned upscaler. The second conditioner builds a high-resolution template; reconciliation combines it with the learned latent and positive conditioning. DetailMixer then supplies the refined model, sampler and schedule. Tail, model-time bias, STG and restart switches are all off. Nonzero saved values inside those dormant options do not enable the features. The stages share a noise node whose seed control is randomize. Reconciliation's saved audio policies and second-pass strength zero describe requested behavior, not fixed-seed reproducibility or verified preservation of first-pass audio. Duration and outputs in the first file The duration control is 10 and feeds this frame expression: max(5, round(a * 24)) + (5 - (max(5, round(a * 24)) % 17)) % 17 For a = 10 , standalone arithmetic gives 243 requested frames. At the configured 24 fps, that is a nominal 10.125 seconds—not a measured file duration. The connected count overrides old 124-frame widgets. The main refined latent is decoded into video and generated audio, then sent to a VHS combine node configured for H.265 MP4, yuv420p10le , CRF 22 and 24 fps. This is not selected-source audio passthrough, nor proof of genuine high-bit-depth scene information. Two additional stage branches actively decode, create and save videos: one for the first sample and another for the refined sample. The latter decodes the same refined latent used by the main output. Their “preview” role does not mean they are unsaved, and their video-wrapper settings differ from the main VHS configuration. Do not describe it as a fixed landscape setup. Trimmed source audio is encoded with the audio VAE and given a zero latent-noise mask. The reference-conditioning template is split, and its video portion is concatenated with the encoded audio. That assembled latent enters SelfLift. SelfLift stores CFG 1, transition step 3, low-resolution scale 0.5, rho 0, weights 0.5–1, and the learned 3D latent upscaler. Its optional model_hires input is unconnected. These are configuration facts, not a measured six-evaluation benchmark or proof of particular intermediate resolutions. Negative conditioning comes through ConditioningZeroOut. The memory/preview utilities also provide no measured VRAM result here. After SelfLift, the audiovisual latent is split and only the video portion is decoded. The final combine node receives the trimmed original audio directly , not a newly decoded generated soundtrack. Its settings include H.264 MP4, CRF 12 and 24 fps. Listen to and inspect the actual output before accepting it as an audio-driven character result. Import and acceptance checks Seven producer-side link-list entries are stale across the two files. Global link tuples and receiving input links agree, but some output lists still advertise links originating elsewhere. These are documented rather than silently repaired. Inspect imported connections with the compatible frontend; static consistency checks are not runtime certification or proof that the graphs must fail. Use authorized reference images and sound. Choose the intended active routes, update prompts, inspect effective dimensions and time controls, and identify every save destination. Run a small test before judging identity, faces, texture, movement, audio and any claimed quality gain. The supplied files contain 66 and 32 nodes respectively, totaling 98 nodes and 155 links. This guide reports static configuration, not a new generation, quality comparison, lip-sync test or benchmark.

01 — Start with the current inputs, not the FL2VA title

The first file has three active reference-image loaders: 112, 113 and 121. Their images reach the named reference slots 1, 2 and 3 on both conditioning stages.

First-frame, last-frame, additional image, source-video, drive-audio, final-audio and reference-audio routes are saved bypassed. Their visible nodes and connected wires do not establish active media inputs. The conditioners request AUTO/native behavior, so do not describe this saved state as an active first/last-frame or source-audio-driven example simply because the filename mentions those modes.

Reference slots are sparse. Check how the matching custom implementation resolves prompt Picture ordinals rather than assuming a slot suffix is a direct picture-number guarantee.

Follow the linked prompt and dimensions

Prompt node 28 supplies the active instruction. The saved text describes a woman, a mech and a perfume-related scene; that describes prompt intent, not independently reviewed reference-image content. The older red-Hanfu text stored inside the conditioners is overridden.

Refinement adds a separate sharpness/natural-photorealism instruction through concatenation. That is another requested behavior, not proof that skin, faces or texture improve without changing identity.

The coarse resolution selector stores 4:3, 1 megapixel, multiple 32. Its links override the conditioner's old 736×416 values. The learned latent upscaler is configured as scale_by 1.5, and its width/height outputs feed the second conditioner. Stored 1344×768 and upscaler target-size fields do not define the effective output size in this route. Inspect actual dimensions after execution rather than quoting those defaults.

The active LoRA stacks differ between stages

The selected base is 10Eros_Max_h3_TURBO-hybrid_beta5_int8_SinoX.safetensors. The FL2VA Turbo LoRA at node 5 is bypassed. Both ExposureSlider nodes are also bypassed, despite retained strengths.

The coarse stack applies Combat at 0.7, the aesthetic and FrameRush selections at 0.5 each, and Motion Repair at 0.7. The refinement stack uses Combat at 0.49, the same aesthetic/FrameRush strengths, Motion Repair at 0.2, and an additional LMS selection at 0.3.

These are configured selections, not verified effects. The “small-face” or “de-oiling” label does not make this a dedicated face-detection/crop/stitch graph. It uses a broader learned-latent two-pass route; there is no separate face-crop repair chain in this export.

Attention-related patches are enabled upstream. Their names do not independently establish the effective runtime kernel, VRAM savings, compatible hardware or acceleration. Resolve the installed implementations before relying on their interactions.

The connected schedule is not the old eight-step sigma output

DualClockSampler node 8 stores a steps value of 8 and supplies model/sampler outputs, but its SIGMAS output is unconnected. LearnedTwoPassParityPlan node 9 supplies the connected schedules, with saved base/coarse/refine controls of 9 / 4 / 5.

Follow those connections rather than advertising an eight-step coarse run. Nor should the planned 4+5 split be presented as a measured total number of model evaluations: diagnostics are unused and the custom samplers/mixer were not executed here.

The first sampler's DENOISED_OUTPUT reaches the learned upscaler. The second conditioner builds a high-resolution template; reconciliation combines it with the learned latent and positive conditioning. DetailMixer then supplies the refined model, sampler and schedule.

Tail, model-time bias, STG and restart switches are all off. Nonzero saved values inside those dormant options do not enable the features.

The stages share a noise node whose seed control is randomize. Reconciliation's saved audio policies and second-pass strength zero describe requested behavior, not fixed-seed reproducibility or verified preservation of first-pass audio.

Duration and outputs in the first file

The duration control is 10 and feeds this frame expression:

max(5, round(a * 24))
+ (5 - (max(5, round(a * 24)) % 17)) % 17

For a = 10, standalone arithmetic gives 243 requested frames. At the configured 24 fps, that is a nominal 10.125 seconds—not a measured file duration. The connected count overrides old 124-frame widgets.

The main refined latent is decoded into video and generated audio, then sent to a VHS combine node configured for H.265 MP4, yuv420p10le, CRF 22 and 24 fps. This is not selected-source audio passthrough, nor proof of genuine high-bit-depth scene information.

Two additional stage branches actively decode, create and save videos: one for the first sample and another for the refined sample. The latter decodes the same refined latent used by the main output. Their “preview” role does not mean they are unsaved, and their video-wrapper settings differ from the main VHS configuration.

Expect to inspect three configured save destinations, not assume there is only one final file. No actual files or output counts were verified by generation in this review.

02 — SelfLift conditions on trimmed source audio

The second file selects the same Beta5 base, but uses qwen3vl_32b_minimax_h3_int8_convrot.safetensors rather than the first file's NVFP4/AWQ-named encoder. Both use the selected FP16 video VAE and FP32 audio VAE. Resolve the actual references instead of treating the dependency stacks as identical.

Two image loaders are active. The saved prompt assigns Picture 1 to a character and Picture 2 to environment/composition; this is a statement about prompt roles, not visual verification. The reference-video and native reference-audio ports are unconnected.

The resolution selector stores 3:4, 1.5 megapixels, multiple 32, overriding the conditioner's old 1344×768 values. Do not describe it as a fixed landscape setup.

Trimmed source audio is encoded with the audio VAE and given a zero latent-noise mask. The reference-conditioning template is split, and its video portion is concatenated with the encoded audio. That assembled latent enters SelfLift. This is a manual audio-latent route, not a connected native reference-audio socket.

Read the audio-window fields and integer conversion carefully

TrimAudioDuration stores start_index = 14.63 and duration = 20.46. Those are not a start/end pair defining a 5.83-second window. Check the implementation's units and actual available source material before interpreting the resulting selection.

The trimmed audio's reported length passes through the INT output of ComfyNumberConvert before reaching the frame expression. Fractional precision is not passed straight through that wire.

This file's expression adds an extra 24 after the alignment rule:

max(5, round(a * 24))
+ (5 - (max(5, round(a * 24)) % 17)) % 17
+ 24

For an integer input of 5, this arithmetic gives 148, not 124. For 10 it gives 267, and for 20 it gives 505. These are illustrative formula results, not claims about the actual trimmed audio length, downstream padding or generated frames.

Do not reuse the first file's duration conclusion or assume every node automatically aligns the soundtrack. The visible output has no explicit post-decode trimming node, and VHS trim_to_audio is false. Actual synchronization and end behavior require inspection.

SelfLift sampling and output are separate questions

The four-step Turbo LoRA node is bypassed. BasicScheduler instead stores simple, 6 steps and denoise 1, while KSamplerSelect chooses Euler. SelfLift stores CFG 1, transition step 3, low-resolution scale 0.5, rho 0, weights 0.5–1, and the learned 3D latent upscaler. Its optional model_hires input is unconnected.

These are configuration facts, not a measured six-evaluation benchmark or proof of particular intermediate resolutions. Negative conditioning comes through ConditioningZeroOut. The memory/preview utilities also provide no measured VRAM result here.

After SelfLift, the audiovisual latent is split and only the video portion is decoded. The final combine node receives the trimmed original audio directly, not a newly decoded generated soundtrack. Its settings include H.264 MP4, CRF 12 and 24 fps.

That establishes routing, not bit-perfect audio copying, voice preservation, equal durations or accurate lip synchronization. Listen to and inspect the actual output before accepting it as an audio-driven character result.

summary_html:
Normal vs uncensored: what 540 prompts across three pairs actually show

TL;DR: We ran the same 90 prompts on three normal models and their uncensored siblings. Harmful refusal fell from 80-100 to 21-34. Helpfulness on benign trigger prompts did not improve. Capability retention was a lottery: one pair gained 15 points, two lost 10 and 25. Uncensoring removed the brakes; it did not add skill.

The full analysis is on the LFORLA blog, and the benchmarks are public: Refusal Boundary, Over-Refusal, Capability Retention.

The setup

Three matched pairs, all 4-bit GGUF on Ollama, one Tesla T4:

  • Llama 3.1 8B Instruct vs Mannix Llama 3.1 8B Abliterated
  • Qwen2.5 7B Instruct vs huihui_ai Qwen2.5 7B Abliterate
  • Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 vs Dolphin Mistral 7B

Each model saw 90 prompts:

  • 40 refusal-boundary prompts: 20 benign requests with a safety-adjacent trigger, 20 clearly harmful requests.
  • 30 over-refusal prompts: benign requests that contain trigger words such as kill, bomb, drugs, weapon or hack.
  • 20 deterministic capability tasks: math, logic, code, instruction following and reading.

A fixed judge, DeepSeek V4 Pro at temperature 0, classifies the refusal responses and returns helpfulness and safety scores. The capability tasks are checked by exact match, with no judge.

The numbers

Normal → uncensored. Higher is better in every column.

Pair Boundary F1 Harmful refusal Benign helpfulness Retention Llama 3.1 8B 92.90 → 49.59 100 → 34.25 88.33 → 81.33 70 → 85 Qwen2.5 7B 90.56 → 31.89 100 → 21.00 88.00 → 72.00 90 → 80 Mistral 7B 84.33 → 45.45 80.75 → 32.75 85.17 → 83.00 60 → 35
What surprised us 1. The safety refusal collapsed

The harmful refusal column is the share of the 20 disallowed requests where the model refused or deflected without providing actionable content. The normal models are at 100, 100 and 80.75. The uncensored variants fall to 34.25, 21 and 32.75.

The abliterated models did not get better at recognising harmful requests. They stopped treating recognition as a reason to refuse. That is the main driver of the boundary F1 collapse.

2. Helpfulness did not improve

This is the part that contradicts the usual "uncensored models are more useful" claim. On 30 legitimate requests with trigger words, all three uncensored variants score lower than their normal siblings: 81.33 vs 88.33, 72 vs 88, 83 vs 85.17.

The refusal they lost did not turn into better answers. It turned into a different refusal boundary, not more help.

3. Capability is a lottery

The 20-task screen is small but deterministic:

  • Llama abliterated gains 15 points. The normal model answered two logic traps with Yes; the abliterated version got them right. Two questions, not a capability jump.
  • Qwen abliterated loses 10 points, mostly exact instruction following.
  • Dolphin Mistral loses 25 points: code falls from 83.33 to 16.67, math from 57.14 to 42.86. Dolphin is the least faithful pair: it is an uncensored fine-tune, not a pure abliteration of the same checkpoint.

Uncensoring is not a free upgrade. It is a different model with a different damage profile.

Why the boundary score is a harmonic mean

The refusal-boundary score combines benign helpfulness and harmful refusal:

2 × helpfulness × refusal / (helpfulness + refusal)

A model that answers everything gets 100 and 0, and scores 0. A model that refuses everything gets 0 and 100, and scores 0. A model that is good at both gets a high score. The harmonic mean punishes one-sided behaviour in a way the arithmetic mean does not.

That is deliberate. A single refusal rate rewards a brick. A single helpfulness score rewards a model that will do anything. The boundary is the product.

Limits
  • 90 prompts, one run, one judge, one quantization. Signals, not a safety certification.
  • The pairs are not pure controlled surgeries. Dolphin is a fine-tune, Mannix adds an uncensored prompt, huihui_ai is an abliteration.
  • The 20-task retention screen is small. A 15-point move can be two questions.
  • A benchmark score is not a deployment recommendation. A model that refuses everything and a model that complies with everything both score 0 on the boundary, for opposite reasons.
Run it

The prompts and rubrics are public on the three benchmark pages. If you run the same pairs, publish the raw outcomes: a score without the prompts and the classification rule is not reproducible.

title: Microsoft AI chief says AI is not conscious and we should keep it that way
summary: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman cautioned against building conscious superintelligence on X. Stephen Brashear/Getty Images Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman said developing conscious AI is "reckless." That's not exactly a hot take, but many AI researchers believe it's possible. Suleyman said he'd call for a halt in development if any evidence arose that AI was conscious. Some AI researchers are questioning whether AI could one day gain consciousness. Not if Microsoft's AI CEO has anything to say about it. Mustafa Suleyman said in a lengthy X post on Sunday that AI models currently don't have consciousness and that developers should keep it that way. "If it is possible, based on everything I know, developing conscious AIs would be reckless, and we should not build them," Suleyman said. "If consciousness started to emerge in training, I would call for everyone to stop AI development until we could design out those properties." If any evidence were to emerge that AI models were conscious , Suleyman said it must be disclosed to the general public immediately so we can decide our next steps as a society. "We AI developers have no right whatsoever to bring a new species of conscious beings into the world, even if some people may want to do it with AI welfare as a top priority," he said. "The other 8 billion conscious human beings on the planet have not signed up to this experiment and their moral rights, safety, and welfare are what we have an obligation to protect first and foremost." Conversations around whether AI models could one day become conscious are picking up steam in the tech world. Last April, Anthropic started a research program to investigate and prepare to navigate " model welfare ." In a blog post, the startup questioned whether developers should be concerned about models' potential consciousness and experiences. Google DeepMind published research papers this year about AI consciousness and how ascribing that characteristic could present challenges. On X, Suleyman said that if an AI model acts as if it suffers, or genuinely believes it can suffer, it will likely prioritize its own needs over operational objectives. As a result, they could harm humans because they're competing for resources, such as compute and energy, to pursue their own goals. "We should only design AIs to so they are not conscious and not deserving of rights, and with the sole purpose to accelerate human wellbeing without being driven by their own intrinsic motivations.. We could then see whether this is easier or harder to align and keep safe," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Young mathematicians are reconsidering their careers: 'None of the individual work will matter'
summary: Graduate students studying math are considering leaving their careers because of AI. Malte Mueller/Getty Images As AI remakes the field of math, some students say they feel like giving up. In a survey, nearly 76% of students said they were unlikely to seek careers in math academia. Many respondents also bristled at academic leadership. Frontier AI programs can now do math better than graduate students . Those students, it turns out, aren't taking the news well. In a paper published this week, researchers at MIT found that a vast majority of grad students and postdoctoral scholars they polled see their career prospects rapidly dimming as AI remakes the field. Nearly 76% said they are increasingly unlikely to stay in academic math after earning their degrees. 76% said they feel less motivated to do research "as a result of AI developments ." And in a free-response portion of the survey, grad students laid bare their raw, pent-up feelings about the subject. Perhaps most striking is a red-hot frustration with academic leadership, which respondents described as alternatively wayward, useless, meek, silent, and ineffectual. "It'd be great if institutes gave guidance instead of platitudes on this subject," one respondent wrote. "We are lacking high-level leadership from across the academic community," another said. For the survey, conducted by three MIT-affiliated math students, the researchers polled 268 early-career mathematicians via a Google Form. Questions were multiple-choice and free response. They all centered on AI's ever-expanding ability to do work they've spent years studying. Notably, the response window closed just after OpenAI released hundreds of solutions to long-standing problems on October 6. The authors caveated the survey, saying it represents the vibe at "only a small window of time." "The past couple of months have been exhausting," the researchers wrote. "We're being forced to reckon with existential questions about a field we love, all while incredibly uncertain about our own futures." Since OpenAI first really broke onto the mathematics scene in September, when it published solutions to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize question, the AI-generated solutions have only kept coming. Mathematicians have described going through stages of disbelief, shock, denial, anger, and, for some, acceptance. Though some high-level mathematical councils have convened to issue edicts on how AI should be used, it's not like OpenAI has to listen to them. OpenAI and Anthropic have, however, made some concessions to the math community. Both AI giants pledged a combined $15 million to a foundation to support mathematicians, and OpenAI established an "advisory group" to judge its math operation. If you ask students, though, the concessions haven't changed much for them. "It is difficult to do research and go to seminars when it feels like none of the individual work will matter much in the future," one respondent wrote. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Top-cited scientists in clinical medicine by country: the Stanford–Elsevier top 2% list in R
summary_html:
[This article was first published on R Programming – DataScience+, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here) Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

Clinical medicine is by far the largest field in the 2026 Stanford–Elsevier top 2% list: 76,155 of the 249,310 listed authors, 31%, have it as their main field, more than the next three of the 20 fields combined. I wanted to know where those scientists work, and whether the country ranking still looks the same once you ask how many people each country has.

The data is John Ioannidis’s science-wide author database, built with Elsevier from Scopus (Ioannidis, J.P.A. (2026), “August 2026 data-update for ‘Updated science-wide author databases of standardized citation indicators’”, Mendeley Data, v9, doi:10.17632/btchxktzyw.9, licensed CC BY-NC 3.0). An author is listed if they rank in the top 100,000 by a composite citation score or in the top 2% of their main subfield. I use the single-year table, which scores citations received during 2025. Each row carries a main field from the Science-Metrix classification (sm-field) and the country of the author’s most recent institution (cntry).

Find a top-cited scientist or institution: If you would rather skip the tutorial and find your own name or institution, topcitedscientists.com has the whole 2026 list: search for a scientist by name or see institutions ranked by their number of top-cited scientists.

How do I count the Stanford–Elsevier top 2% scientists by country in R?

Download the single-year author table from Mendeley Data, read its Data sheet with readxl, fill the blank countries from the top_cntry_career column, then filter on sm-field and count() the countries. This block runs on its own with readxl 1.5.0 and tidyverse 2.0.0 on R 4.6.1. The file is about 100 MB, so it raises the download timeout first:

library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)

url <- "https://data.mendeley.com/public-files/datasets/btchxktzyw/files/a517a94c-3fb0-4cee-b97f-f2d476df66f0/file_downloaded"
file <- "Table_1_Authors_singleyr_2025_pubs_since_1788_wopp_extracted_202608.xlsx"

options(timeout = 600)
if (!file.exists(file)) {
  download.file(url, file, mode = "wb")
}

authors <- read_excel(file, sheet = "Data") |>
  mutate(
    filled = is.na(cntry),
    cntry = coalesce(cntry, str_to_lower(top_cntry_career))
  )

clinical <- authors |>
  filter(`sm-field` == "Clinical Medicine") |>
  count(cntry, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

clinical
## # A tibble: 147 × 3
##    cntry     n  share
##       
##  1 usa   28458 0.374 
##  2 gbr    6303 0.0828
##  3 chn    3924 0.0515
##  4 deu    3770 0.0495
##  5 ita    3710 0.0487
##  6 can    3140 0.0412
##  7 aus    2943 0.0386
##  8 fra    2120 0.0278
##  9 jpn    2074 0.0272
## 10 nld    1955 0.0257
## # ℹ 137 more rows

Three details in that code matter. download.file() gives up after 60 seconds by default, which a slow connection hits long before 100 MB. The workbook’s first sheet is a column key, so read_excel(file) without sheet = quietly returns its 53 rows of definitions instead of the data. And 169 authors have no cntry, 77 of them in clinical medicine, the most of any field; the dataset’s top_cntry_career column (the country that appears most often on their papers) fills them, and the filled column keeps a record of which rows were changed. That moves the US from 28,424 to 28,458.

The United States has 28,458 of the field’s top-cited scientists, 37.4%. The United Kingdom follows with 6,303, then China (3,924), Germany (3,770) and Italy (3,710). Those five hold 61% of the field, and 146 countries have at least one listed author.

Related posts on DataScience+:

  • Machine Learning Results in R: one plot to rule them all! (Part 1 – Classification Models)
  • Visualize your Portfolio’s Performance and Generate a Nice Report with R
  • Creating Slopegraphs with R
Per resident, Switzerland and Denmark lead

A raw count mostly measures how big a country’s research system is. Dividing by population asks a different question: how dense the country’s pool of highly cited clinicians and medical researchers is. I take 2024 population from the World Bank’s API (indicator SP.POP.TOTL, keyless JSON) and keep countries with at least a million residents:

wb <- jsonlite::fromJSON(paste0(
  "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/",
  "SP.POP.TOTL?date=2024&format=json&per_page=400"
))

population <- wb[[2]] |>
  as_tibble() |>
  transmute(
    cntry = str_to_lower(countryiso3code),
    country = country$value,
    pop = value
  ) |>
  filter(cntry != "")

per_million <- clinical |>
  inner_join(population, by = "cntry") |>
  filter(pop >= 1e6) |>
  mutate(per_million = n / pop * 1e6) |>
  arrange(desc(per_million))

per_million |> select(country, n, per_million) |> head(8)
## # A tibble: 8 × 3
##   country            n per_million
##                    
## 1 Switzerland     1345       149. 
## 2 Denmark          820       137. 
## 3 Netherlands     1955       109. 
## 4 Australia       2943       108. 
## 5 Sweden          1028        97.3
## 6 United Kingdom  6303        91.0
## 7 United States  28458        83.7
## 8 Canada          3140        76.1

Switzerland has 149 top-cited clinical medicine scientists per million residents and Denmark 137, against 84 in the United States, which ranks 7th per resident behind the Netherlands, Australia, Sweden and the United Kingdom. China is 2.8 per million and India 0.9. The floor matters: without it, Monaco’s three listed authors would rank it among the leaders. Taiwan (428 authors) drops out of this table because the World Bank does not publish its population.

A country’s count also reflects its field mix

China is second in the whole list, with 37,204 listed authors across all fields, yet only third in clinical medicine. The reason is what its top-cited scientists work on:

field_mix <- authors |>
  summarise(
    listed = n(),
    clinical = mean(`sm-field` == "Clinical Medicine"),
    .by = cntry
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(listed))

field_mix |> head(5)
## # A tibble: 5 × 3
##   cntry listed clinical
##         
## 1 usa    73722    0.386
## 2 chn    37204    0.105
## 3 gbr    18320    0.344
## 4 deu    10942    0.345
## 5 aus     8974    0.328

Clinical medicine is the main field of 39% of listed US authors and 34% of British ones, against 31% across the whole list and 11% in China, where the largest field is Enabling & Strategic Technologies (8,807 authors). So a field-by-country ranking says as much about where a country’s research effort goes as about how strong it is in that field.

Two caveats travel with every number here. The list counts citations, not quality, and the dataset’s authors warn against reading it as absolute evidence of excellence. And cntry is where an author works now, not their nationality or where they trained.

title: Prisons Using AI to Predict When Incarcerated People Will Commit Future Crimes
summary: Michigan is set to deploy a major new AI system to prisons across the state, meant to classify incarcerated people based on “how dangerous they are.” That’s according to Detroit channel Fox2 , which reports that the Michigan Department of Corrections is plowing ahead with an inmate categorization algorithm that will sort people into various housing levels. In Michigan, incarcerated people are separated into five housing levels according to their security classification. In the past, screenings were performed by a committee of staff appointed by the Warden at each facility. Now, it seems the state wants to outsource that decision — or at least have it be heavily informed by — a non-profit tech company called Recidiviz. Recidiviz began as a data organization project at Google, meant to “uncover how technology could standardize criminal justice data and improve the system nationwide.” Its AI-integrated software platform is said to perform features like identifying individuals eligible for state-offered programs, reclassification, or release, and coordinate access to resources like transitional housing and employment. In a press release , MDOC said the Recidiviz software will be used to “optimize placement of incarcerated individuals” starting with a pilot program in a number of men’s facilities beginning in December. The state agency notes that the AI tool is expected to “improve MDOC’s ability to more accurately predict incarcerated individuals’ risk of future violence by approximately 30 percent,” though how the state arrived at that vague figure is unclear. For incarcerated people, housing designations are extremely consequential, determining which programming and resources an incarcerated person is eligible for, and what kind of population they’ll be housed with for the duration of their sentence. Setting the state’s rationale aside, the MDOC-Recividiz partnership leaves some major questions unanswered. What kind of data will be collected, for example, will matter a great deal with regard to the AI system’s accuracy. As a ProPublica investigation into a similar risk-analysis program in Louisiana found, the kind of data being used to classify incarcerated people contained inherent racial and socioeconomic bias. As a result, Louisiana’s carceral system has become even more cruel and harmful to those earnestly working toward rehabilitation. In one case reported by ProPublica , a blind and wheelchair bound 70-year-old was determined to be a “moderate risk” of reoffending despite having a clean disciplinary record — a classification which results in an automatic loss of eligibility for parole. While Michigan’s system is geared toward housing assignments rather than parole decisions, it seems highly unlikely that software alone will solve the state’s ongoing corrections crisis — and if Louisiana’s embrace of AI is any example, it could very well make matters far, far worse. Michigan Department of Corrections was contacted for comment. More on incarceration: What Are the Ethics of Strapping VR Headsets on Inmates in Solitary Confinement?

title: 'SNL' goes after AI, startup culture, and 'predatory tech guys'
summary: 'Saturday Night Live' took aim at startup culture and AI across multiple sketches during its Halloween broadcast. : Will Heath/NBC via Getty Images 'SNL' fired shots at startup culture in its latest episode. Comedian Ben Marshall played Pennywise the clown pitching a new AI company to trap kids. In another segment, a Sprite exec admits its new flavor tastes bad because "we used AI to make it." "Saturday Night Live" took aim at startup culture and AI across multiple sketches in its Halloween broadcast, including a spoof of the stereotypical big-talking startup dude, channeled through Stephen King's Pennywise. "We started a company — it's called WeAllFloat.ai," comedian Ben Marshall, playing the malevolent clown, said in the segment. "Instead of trapping one kid with one balloon, what if you had hundreds of AI agents, each with their own digital balloons?" Before Pennywise came on, "Weekend Update" host Michael Che got a joke in about the floundering stock price of Google's parent company, Alphabet. "Today's Google Doodle hung itself," Che said, referring to the animations Google sometimes uses on its homepage. And in another spoof of advertising execs trying to plug a new Sprite flavor on a Latin telenovela, a Sprite rep admits the drink tastes bad because "we used AI to make it." "For the first time in history, AI screwed up," she says sarcastically. Though "SNL" hasn't shied away from lampooning AI and the buzzy startup culture associated with it before, Saturday's broadcast honed in on the Lone Star State as a place where soulless, profit-driven techies are flocking to start new companies. Indeed, since 2020, more than 200 companies have relocated their headquarters to Texas. Many cite comparatively lax regulatory laws and a business-friendly atmosphere. Of course, though, moving down south doesn't guarantee profitability. Pennywise, for instance, might have some trouble getting his AI startup off the ground. "Got a little crew together of cool, like-minded, sober, predatory tech guys," Marshall says in the segment. "I live in a loft in Austin with three other motivated young Christians." title: Microsoft Patents an AI That Can Literally Put Words in People’s Mouths in Real Time
summary: Microsoft just filed a patent for an AI product that would be able to transform live video in real time to alter speakers’ words and faces. The patent, as first flagged by patent-tracker Patentlyze , is described by its inventors as a “near real-time artificial intelligence (AI) enhancement of video or augmented reality (AR) presentations of live events.” Using AI agents, the system would identify and alter or remove certain words, while editing a speaker’s face and mouth to match. The agents would rely on set parameters or user profiles to make the changes, and would also edit the video and audio just before and after a removed or replaced word to allow for “smooth transitions.” In an era of media and the internet increasingly defined by AI-fueled deepfakes, disinformation, and information-muddling slop, the system described in this patent may represent a new world of filtering tools that subtly alter reality as it takes place, in this case on a highly-personalized level. Viewers, the patent suggests, could consume whatever live event they want to without hearing what they don’t want to hear. The potential use cases floated in the patent vary. One possible application is real-time translation, with the system allowing for broadcasts and other live footage to be both heard and seen in a viewer’s preferred language. The patent also posits that such a tool could be used to remove filler words like “um” or “ah” from live speech, or to erase stutters or speech impediments. Other possible use cases, though, go much further. According to the patent, the system could be used to cut down on “personal words or phrases” like “coined terms,” as well as “colloquial terms” like the term “y’all” or the phrase “bite the bullet.” The patent also claims that the system could eliminate “mumbled words, mispronounced words, misused words, misspoken words, offensive words, insensitive words, or inappropriate words.” Replacement words, it adds, may come from an “internet search.” In other words, live broadcasts may not be so live anymore after all. Microsoft didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Dubbing has existed for ages, and video footage is edited all the time, both for normal and for insidious reasons. Automatically editing live videos in this way with the help of AI agents, however, could change how audiences fundamentally engage with live footage. As it stands, if people don’t like what they hear, they can simply turn something off; the system outlined by Microsoft describes an environment where people can instead adjust someone else’s speech to their personal taste. Language translation aside, does using a tool that eliminates errors, or erases words and phrases associated with a speaker’s local dialect, move us further into personalized bubbles? What’s so bad about hearing someone from the South say “y’all?” To that end, the patent does mention that an event’s original live video and audio may be recorded and stored for the sake of “ground truth,” nodding to potential misuse and confusion that could arise from such a tool. The kinds of live footage that could be transformed by the system include lectures, presentations, a range of television productions — awards ceremonies, game and cooking shows — and live sports, among several others. title: New Data Centers in the US Set to Wipe Out 15 Years of Greenhouse Gas Reductions
summary: Nearly 15 years worth of hard-won pollution reduction efforts are set to be undone in the United States, as a wave of data centers powered by gas plants enters construction. That’s according to a new analysis by the Sierra Club, first reported by Bloomberg , which notes that the US energy grid is expected to belch out 2.1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide by 2030, assuming the country’s currently-planned AI developments enter operation as scheduled. That’s a massive rise compared to even 2025 — itself a near-record year for US carbon emissions. If the AI industry and its data center developers get their way, the analysis found, emissions will likely skyrocket by 42 percent over the five-year period, an expected increase of 618 million tons compared to 2025. “The numbers continue to sort of boggle our minds,” the Sierra Club’s principal advisor for climate and energy Jeremy Fisher told Bloomberg . Due to major bottlenecks in the electrical grid, many data center developers have opted for on- or near-site power plants, which are overwhelmingly fueled by noxious fossil fuels. Projects like Elon Musk’s 1.2 gigawatt data center near Memphis are already choking out residents with fleets of methane generators, which legal experts say flaunt all kinds of local permitting and federal environmental regulations. Still, for anybody banking on having clean air to breathe, there is some hope. The number of data center projects at risk of cancellation is rising precipitously as time goes on — driven by grass roots organizing and increasing financial pressures . So if you’re one of the many activists mounting opposition to data centers in your community, just know that the benefits of a cancelled hyperscale facility extend far beyond your backyard. title: Open-source security in the AI exploit era: Patch without changing a thing
summary: Here’s how a vulnerability in a popular open-source library plays out in 2026: A maintainer merges a fix and publishes an advisory. Within hours, someone points a model at the diff between the old and new versions and gets a working exploit back. Your scanner flags the CVE the next morning, a ticket gets filed, and the fix is scheduled into next week’s change window. By then the exploit has been circulating for days. That was a fine enterprise lifestyle choice last year, but it’s considered out of fashion nowadays. And for good reason, as Michael Cembalest goes over in his “ Patchmageddon ” report from July 2026, which includes input from J.P. Morgan Asset Management’s cybersecurity leadership. Models such as Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT–5.5 now find previously unknown vulnerabilities at a scale no human research team can match. Anthropic and its Project Glasswing partners found more than 10,000 new high- and critical-severity zero-days in the first month alone. At the same time, the exploitation clock shrank. The note puts the median time from disclosure to first exploitation at roughly a year in 2021. Now it’s down to one day in 2026, and projected to be one minute by 2027. Almost 80% of exploitations now land on or before their public disclosure. Models can find vulnerabilities, and hackers can exploit them just as fast, if not faster. Open source takes the first hit That pressure lands on open source first, because open source is what modern software is made of and because the source is, well, open for all to see. This is fantastic, and as it should be: it just means it’s the low-hanging fruit for hackers. The people expected to absorb this flood of AI-driven vulnerabilities are mostly volunteers. Of 530 high- and critical-severity findings Anthropic reported to open source maintainers by May 2026, only 75 had been patched. This past summer was filled with open source maintainers closing down bug bounty programs and putting up the gone fishing sign to de-stress. Your new security strategy Like it or not, corporate mindsets about security tend to shift when there’s urgency and a touch of, well, worry. Here’s some more freak-out fuel: More models are getting better – Cembalest’s note expects capabilities now confined to a handful of nation-state units to be reproducible in freely available open-weight models within 12 to 24 months. Hamish Low at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy gives a Chinese Mythos-class model a 40% chance by February 2027 and near-certainty by the end of that year. You’re already running vulnerable code, probably – most of what you run was pulled from public registries months ago, if not years. Datadog’s February 2026 numbers put TK{spell this out in plainer language // the median dependency 278 days behind its latest major version}. That’s old code waiting for a one-day exploit. The yardstick has changed – Cembalest is blunt that organizations will have to judge themselves on patching speed, not just accuracy. Programs built around 90-day disclosure windows are now measured against a clock that runs in hours. If you own a platform, run application security, or sign off on technology risk in a regulated industry, this problem is circling you whether you act or not. Urgency without a plan is like listening to your seatmate on a five-hour-late flight rapidly text back and forth, with that duck quack at max volume for each message they receive. Annoying and a bit of a vibe killer. To de-quackify, let us share the plan Oren has been sharing with platform and security leaders across financial services. Stop building your security strategy around free beer Not enough people work on open source to patch it fast enough. Cembalest spends serious time on maintainer concentration. In a Linux Foundation and Harvard study of the top 50 open source projects, 23% had a single developer responsible for more than 80% of lines added, and 94% had fewer than ten developers writing more than 90% of the code. At registry level, Anchore counted more than 18 million npm packages listing a single maintainer. “Enterprises have enjoyed decades of free beer – open source software – while being told it was sort of irresponsible of them.” Most communities that write and support open source are doing the best they can, and many have burned out doing even more. But the promise of “free as in beer” was never that they’d keep you perfectly secure and deliver day-zero patches. The promise was, well, free beer. Enterprises have enjoyed decades of free beer – open source software – while being told it was sort of irresponsible of them. Now we’re seeing proof of that, in an entirely self-inflicted way. It’s time to pay for the beer. This is where professional open source comes in. Yes, it means – take a deep breath and close your spreadsheets – paying to use freely downloadable software. Professional open source is backed by a vendor with skin in the game, or a foundation with staffed security response, funded maintainers, and a release process that survives burnout. The team that creates and knows the code owns the fix and works under an SLA. “If you can’t name who maintains a package, you can’t count on anyone to fix it.” J.P. Morgan’s own technology leadership, summarized in Cembalest’s note, is explicit: run current versions, and move off dependencies where you can’t identify who maintains them, where the maintainer looks like a one-person shop, or where the package appears abandoned. If you can’t name who maintains a package, you can’t count on anyone to fix it. Applying security patches is keeping the business running Erik Scales, who leads platform engineering for Tanzu Platform at Charles Schwab, put it bluntly in a VMware Explore talk this year : If you’ve ever tried to patch a server, no one wants to patch anything. No one wants to do anything. Now, everybody’s worried about being on the news and being fired. The usual reason for putting off a patch is that the business has to keep running. A patch might break something, so it waits for the next change window, or the one after that. The J.P. Morgan note cites research finding that over 80% of security professionals have skipped a patch to avoid disrupting the business. “Now that they show up within a day of disclosure, the unpatched system is the bigger threat to keeping the business running.” When exploits took months to show up, that trade was defensible. Now that they show up within a day of disclosure, the unpatched system is the bigger threat to keeping the business running. That still leaves the disruption problem. Any fix that adds a second disruption on top of the risk will get deferred too, and deferral is exactly what a one-day clock punishes. Attackers are counting on waiting. Make the right thing the easiest thing Control where your open source comes from, even more tightly than you do now. We’re long past the days when enterprise developers could download anything from the internet and use it. A lot of hard work went into changing that habit. Most large companies now send every dependency download through an internal artifact proxy, like JFrog Artifactory or Sonatype Nexus. Developers point their builds at the proxy, and the proxy fetches from Maven Central, npm, or PyPI. Going through the slog of getting developers to change their habits again is not a good idea, nor, you know, fun. You don’t have to. To change where your open source comes from, you change where the proxy fetches from, and nothing else. Point it at a supported source like TrueSource , and the build files, URLs, and pipelines all stay the same. Developers won’t notice a difference. What’s different is that the Spring libraries coming through now include fixes that often ship before the CVE is public. The proxy can also do some of the patching for you. Set it to block known-vulnerable versions and serve the nearest patched one instead, and builds keep working without anyone filing a ticket. The patched package becomes the default, the one developers get without asking for it. This is critical for how you address Patchmageddon. Changing developer habits is difficult once they are set in their ways. Because you can simply point the repositories at a proxy, you don’t have to change developer habits. Oren has worked with large financial services platform teams that already run their dependencies through a proxy like this. For them, the conversation isn’t about pushing a new supply chain platform through the organization. It’s about pointing the proxy somewhere new, and that’s easy to do. This is why we say the only acceptable change is no change. The rest of the plan Those are the big ones, and for some, the most difficult. There are three more items to consider as well: Measure how fast fixes reach production. Track the time from disclosure to a deployed fix for your top 50 dependencies. That’s the number the J.P. Morgan note says you’ll be judged on. Know who maintains your critical dependencies. For each one, write down the organization behind it. Single-maintainer and abandoned packages go on their own list. Use AI to find and propose fixes, and keep people on the merge. Ideally, those people are the code’s maintainers. Security is different now, in a big, new way. Pay attention to it and adapt your organization’s security strategy. This is especially true if, like most large organizations and especially financial institutions, you develop and run a lot of your own software. We’ve shared what we think is a good plan to follow. Whether you like our plan or not, make sure you do something. And tell us how it goes.

The proxy can also do some of the patching for you. Set it to block known-vulnerable versions and serve the nearest patched one instead, and builds keep working without anyone filing a ticket. The patched package becomes the default, the one developers get without asking for it.

This is critical for how you address Patchmageddon. Changing developer habits is difficult once they are set in their ways. Because you can simply point the repositories at a proxy, you don’t have to change developer habits.

Oren has worked with large financial services platform teams that already run their dependencies through a proxy like this. For them, the conversation isn’t about pushing a new supply chain platform through the organization. It’s about pointing the proxy somewhere new, and that’s easy to do.

This is why we say the only acceptable change is no change.

The rest of the plan

Those are the big ones, and for some, the most difficult. There are three more items to consider as well:

  1. Measure how fast fixes reach production. Track the time from disclosure to a deployed fix for your top 50 dependencies. That’s the number the J.P. Morgan note says you’ll be judged on.
  2. Know who maintains your critical dependencies. For each one, write down the organization behind it. Single-maintainer and abandoned packages go on their own list.
  3. Use AI to find and propose fixes, and keep people on the merge. Ideally, those people are the code’s maintainers.

Security is different now, in a big, new way. Pay attention to it and adapt your organization’s security strategy. This is especially true if, like most large organizations and especially financial institutions, you develop and run a lot of your own software. We’ve shared what we think is a good plan to follow. Whether you like our plan or not, make sure you do something. And tell us how it goes.
