title: AWS Kiro Core: Building Smarter Applications with Agentic Development
summary: AI coding tools are changing how developers build software. Today, we can ask AI to generate functions, explain errors, create APIs, write tests, and even help build complete applications. But there is one important problem: generating code does not automatically mean building good software. A reliable application still needs clear requirements, proper architecture, consistent coding standards, security, testing, and maintainability. This is where AWS Kiro becomes interesting. Kiro is an agentic development environment from AWS that helps developers go beyond simple AI code generation. It introduces structured development workflows through specifications, steering documents, agent hooks, MCP integrations, and specialized agent capabilities. Instead of simply asking AI to write code, developers can guide an agent through understanding a project, defining requirements, designing a solution, implementing features, and validating the results. In this article, we'll explore AWS Kiro Core, understand its most useful capabilities, and build a practical Student Management Portal feature using a hands-on approach. 1. What Is AWS Kiro? AWS Kiro is an agentic integrated development environment designed to help developers build and maintain software with AI assistance. Traditional AI coding assistants generally focus on answering questions, generating code snippets, and completing code. Kiro takes a broader approach by supporting different stages of software development. Imagine that you want to add a student search feature to an existing application. You might initially ask: Add a search feature to my Student Management Portal. But several questions remain: Should users search by name, email, or student ID? Should the feature support filters? How should pagination work? Which APIs need to change? What validation is required? How should authorization work? Which automated tests should be added? Kiro helps developers approach these questions systematically. A simplified agentic development workflow looks like this: Business Requirement | v Requirements | v Technical Design | v Implementation Tasks | v Code Generation | v Testing & Review | v Working Feature The key idea is to understand the problem before implementing the solution. 2. Core AWS Kiro Capabilities Let's explore the capabilities that make Kiro useful for modern software engineering. 2.1 Spec-Driven Development One of Kiro's most interesting capabilities is spec-driven development. In many AI coding workflows, developers provide a prompt and immediately receive generated code. That approach can work for small tasks, but larger features need proper planning. Spec-driven development introduces a structured process before implementation. A typical specification contains three important artifacts. requirements.md Describes what needs to be built. It can include: User stories. Functional requirements. Acceptance criteria. Expected application behavior. Validation requirements. design.md Describes how the feature should be implemented. It may include: Application architecture. Database changes. API design. Component responsibilities. Security considerations. Technical decisions. tasks.md Breaks implementation into manageable development tasks. Example: Student Search Feature 1. Review the existing student model. 2. Review the current student API. 3. Add search functionality. 4. Add course filtering. 5. Add enrollment status filtering. 6. Implement pagination. 7. Add input validation. 8. Write automated tests. 9. Verify existing functionality. The developer can review these files, correct requirements, and approve the plan before implementation begins. Why is this useful? It reduces ambiguity and gives developers more control over what the agent is going to build. Rather than discovering missing requirements after code generation, teams can identify them during planning. 2.2 Steering Documents One common problem with AI coding assistants is repeatedly explaining the same project details. For example: Which programming language does the project use? Which framework is being used? What database is configured? What coding standards should be followed? Where should new files be created? How should errors be handled? Kiro uses steering documents to provide persistent project-specific guidance. A typical project structure looks like this: my-application/ │ ├── frontend/ ├── backend/ ├── tests/ │ └── .kiro/ └── steering/ ├── product.md ├── tech.md └── structure.md Example tech.md : # Technology Standards - Backend: Python FastAPI - Frontend: React - Database: PostgreSQL - API architecture: REST - Testing framework: Pytest # Development Guidelines - Follow existing project conventions. - Validate user inputs. - Use environment variables for configuration. - Never hardcode credentials. - Write automated tests for new features. - Avoid unnecessary dependencies. - Follow least-privilege security principles. Steering documents should describe the actual project rather than introducing technologies that the application does not use. Productivity benefit: Developers spend less time repeating project instructions, and AI-generated changes can follow established development standards more consistently. 2.3 Agent Hooks Developers frequently perform repetitive activities: Running tests after modifying code. Checking coding standards. Reviewing changes. Updating documentation. Validating configuration files. Kiro Hooks can help automate development activities based on configured events. Example workflow: Developer Changes Code | v Agent Hook | v Run Test Command | v Review Test Results | v Developer Reviews Fixes For example, you can configure a workflow that runs relevant backend tests after backend files are modified. Hooks can reduce manual effort and help developers maintain consistent workflows. However, automation should be configured carefully. Running tests is generally low risk, while deploying code or modifying production infrastructure requires stronger safeguards. 2.4 Model Context Protocol (MCP) The Model Context Protocol, commonly called MCP, provides a standardized way for AI agents to interact with external tools and services through configured MCP servers. This is useful because developers often need information outside their local codebase. For example, when developing an AWS application, you might need to: Find AWS service documentation. Understand an API operation. Check configuration requirements. Investigate integration problems. Access connected developer tools. With an appropriately configured MCP server, Kiro can interact with supported external tools and retrieve relevant information. The AWS Documentation MCP server is particularly useful for AWS-related development workflows. Example prompt: Research the best AWS services for deploying this application. Explain: 1. Suitable AWS services. 2. Deployment architecture. 3. Security considerations. 4. Networking requirements. 5. Cost considerations. 6. Monitoring and logging options. Use the available AWS documentation tools. Do not create or deploy AWS resources. Only provide a technical recommendation. MCP does not automatically grant unrestricted access to external systems. Available tools and permissions depend on the server configuration and the permissions granted to the agent. 2.5 Agent Skills and Powers Skills and Powers help extend agent capabilities with specialized instructions, knowledge, and tools. Imagine that you regularly perform: AWS architecture reviews. Application security checks. Documentation generation. Infrastructure development. Code quality reviews. Instead of explaining the entire workflow every time, you can use reusable specialized capabilities. Some practical areas include: AWS development. Security reviews. Documentation generation. Infrastructure development. Code quality checks. The goal is to make agents more useful for specialized engineering responsibilities. 2.6 Custom Agents and Permissions Different software development tasks require different responsibilities. For example: Agent role Responsibility Code Review Agent Review code changes and identify issues Testing Agent Identify missing tests and validate functionality Infrastructure Agent Review infrastructure configuration Documentation Agent Generate and maintain technical documentation Custom agents can help organize work around these responsibilities. Permissions are equally important. An AI agent should not automatically receive unrestricted access to application files, credentials, databases, or cloud infrastructure. Developers should configure access carefully and review high-impact operations before execution. This becomes particularly important when using agents for AWS development and deployment workflows. 3. Kiro IDE, CLI, Web, Mobile, and Crew Kiro's agent experience extends beyond a traditional code editor. Depending on availability and product status, developers can explore different Kiro surfaces. Kiro IDE: An integrated development environment for coding, specifications, steering documents, hooks, and agent workflows. Kiro CLI: A command-line experience for interacting with agents directly from the terminal. Kiro Web: A browser-based experience for agent-driven development tasks. Kiro Mobile: A mobile experience for interacting with development tasks and agent activity. Check the official documentation for current availability and preview status. Kiro Crew: An agent experience focused on ongoing work, reusable context, and task-oriented workflows. These experiences provide more flexibility for developers who work across different environments. Check the official Kiro documentation for the latest feature availability. 4. Vibe Coding vs. Spec-Driven Development Two useful approaches to building applications with Kiro are vibe coding and spec-driven development. Vibe Coding Vibe coding is an interactive approach where developers describe what they want and work with AI to generate or modify code. Example: Create a modern student management dashboard. Include: - A sidebar. - A student overview section. - Student information cards. - A searchable student table. - A responsive layout. Use the existing frontend framework. This approach is useful for: Quick prototypes. UI improvements. Small features. Experiments. Learning new technologies. Spec-Driven Development Spec-driven development starts with requirements and technical planning. Example: Build a student search feature. Requirements: - Search by name, email, and student ID. - Filter by course and enrollment status. - Support pagination. - Validate user inputs. - Add automated tests. - Follow existing authorization rules. First generate the requirements, technical design, and implementation tasks. Wait for my approval before implementation. This approach is useful for: Complex features. Production applications. Multi-component changes. Team development. Projects with clear acceptance criteria. Neither approach is universally better. Choose based on the complexity and risk of the task. 5. Hands-On Project: Build a Student Search Feature Using Kiro Let's apply these concepts in a practical project. The AWS Kiro Core workshop provides a Student Management Portal learning exercise. We'll use a similar feature to demonstrate how Kiro can help transform a requirement into a working implementation. Project Objective Build a feature that allows users to: Search students by name. Search students by email. Search students by student ID. Filter students by course. Filter students by enrollment status. Navigate results using pagination. See a useful message when no results match. Step 1: Access the AWS Kiro Core Workshop Open the official workshop: https://catalog.us-east-1.prod.workshops.aws/workshops/7aa94656-c586-4ee3-8b5a-5494b3b488b4 Follow the workshop setup instructions and prepare the provided development environment. The workshop uses an AWS Academy lab environment. Follow its specific IAM and environment restrictions. Do not create additional resources or permissions that the lab does not allow. Open the Student Management Portal project in Kiro. Step 2: Ask Kiro to Understand the Existing Application Before making changes, ask Kiro to analyze the project. Use this prompt: Analyze this Student Management Portal project. I want to understand: 1. The frontend architecture. 2. The backend architecture. 3. The database structure. 4. Existing student-related APIs. 5. Current search and filtering functionality. 6. Authentication and authorization. 7. Existing testing approach. Identify the files relevant to implementing a student search and filter feature. Do not modify any files yet. Provide a clear summary of the existing application architecture and development flow. Expected result: Kiro should explain the existing project structure and identify the files relevant to the feature. Review its findings before proceeding. Step 3: Generate Steering Documents Ask Kiro to document the project's technical context. Analyze the existing application and create project steering documents. Create: - product.md - tech.md - structure.md Document: 1. Application purpose. 2. Technology stack. 3. Coding conventions. 4. Project directory structure. 5. Development standards. 6. Testing approach. 7. Security guidelines. Use the existing project as the source of truth. Do not invent technologies or change the existing application architecture. Expected result: Kiro should generate project-specific steering documents. Review the content and correct any inaccurate information. Step 4: Create the Feature Specification Now move to spec-driven development. Use this prompt: Create a specification for a Student Search and Filter feature. Functional requirements: 1. Search students by name. 2. Search students by email. 3. Search students by student ID. 4. Filter students by course. 5. Filter students by enrollment status. 6. Support pagination. 7. Display a message when no students match the search. 8. Validate search inputs. 9. Follow existing authentication and authorization rules. 10. Add automated tests. Generate these artifacts: - requirements.md - design.md - tasks.md Follow the existing application architecture and project steering documents. Do not implement the feature yet. Wait for my review and approval before making code changes. Expected result: Kiro should help produce three specification artifacts. Review the requirements, design decisions, and implementation tasks. Check whether important edge cases are covered, including empty search terms, invalid inputs, duplicate records, and unauthorized access. Step 5: Implement the Feature After reviewing and approving the specification, ask Kiro to implement it. Implement the approved Student Search and Filter specification. Follow the existing project architecture. Work through the implementation tasks in the specified order. For each task: 1. Explain the planned changes. 2. Implement the required functionality. 3. Add or update automated tests. 4. Run relevant tests. 5. Summarize modified files. 6. Report any errors or limitations. Do not modify unrelated functionality. Ask for my approval before any destructive or high-impact operation. Expected result: Kiro should work through the implementation tasks and report the changes. Review the generated code and diffs rather than accepting every change automatically. Step 6: Create an Agent Hook Let's automate part of the development workflow. Use this prompt: Create an agent hook that helps maintain test coverage for the Student Management Portal. When relevant backend files are modified, run the appropriate backend test command. When relevant frontend files are modified, run the appropriate frontend test command. Display test failures clearly. Do not automatically deploy the application. Do not make unrelated code changes. Wait for developer review before applying additional fixes. Configure the hook according to the actual project structure, available hook events, and test commands. Expected result: A reusable automation workflow that helps developers remember to run relevant tests after changes. Step 7: Explore AWS Documentation Through MCP Configure the AWS Documentation MCP server by following the official workshop instructions. Then use this prompt: I am preparing to deploy this application on AWS. Use the available AWS documentation tools to research suitable deployment options. Explain: 1. Suitable AWS services. 2. A possible deployment architecture. 3. Security considerations. 4. Networking requirements. 5. Cost considerations. 6. Monitoring and logging options. Do not create AWS resources or deploy the application. Only provide a technical recommendation. Expected result: Kiro can use the configured documentation tools to help research relevant AWS services and deployment considerations. Review all recommendations against official AWS documentation before applying them. Step 8: Test the Completed Feature Finally, validate the implementation. Use this checklist: [ ] Search by student name works. [ ] Search by email works. [ ] Search by student ID works. [ ] Course filtering works. [ ] Enrollment status filtering works. [ ] Pagination works. [ ] Empty search results are handled correctly. [ ] Invalid inputs are handled safely. [ ] Authorization rules are respected. [ ] Automated tests pass. [ ] Existing application functionality still works. What Have We Learned? By completing this project, you will understand how to use Kiro for: Understanding an existing codebase. Creating project steering documents. Defining feature requirements. Designing implementation plans. Generating and reviewing code. Automating development checks. Connecting external documentation through MCP. Validating the final implementation. This is a practical way to move from simply asking AI to generate code toward using an agentic development workflow. 6. How Kiro Can Improve Developer Productivity Let's connect Kiro's capabilities with common software development challenges. Development challenge Kiro capability Potential benefit Unclear requirements Spec-driven development Better feature planning Repeating project instructions Steering documents Consistent project context Repetitive development checks Agent Hooks Less manual work Finding external documentation MCP integrations Reduced context switching Repeated specialized workflows Skills and Powers Reusable expertise Different development responsibilities Custom agents Focused workflows Managing agent activity Agent session management Better task visibility Unwanted access to files or tools Permissions More control over agent actions The biggest opportunity is reducing the time spent switching between planning, coding, documentation, testing, and troubleshooting. However, productivity should not be measured only by how quickly code is generated. A better measure is how quickly a developer can deliver a correct, tested, secure, and maintainable feature. 7. Best Practices for Using Kiro in Real Projects Here are some practical recommendations for developers and engineering teams. 1. Understand the existing codebase first. Ask Kiro to analyze the application architecture before requesting major changes. 2. Write clear prompts. Include expected behavior, constraints, validation requirements, and edge cases. 3. Review specifications before implementation. An incorrect requirement can produce incorrect code. Review the requirements and design before proceeding. 4. Keep steering documents updated. Outdated technical context can lead to incorrect implementation decisions. 5. Automate repetitive tasks. Use hooks for routine checks, but keep risky operations under developer control. 6. Apply least-privilege access. Do not give agents unrestricted access to production environments, credentials, or cloud resources. 7. Test AI-generated code. Run unit tests, integration tests, security checks, and application-level validation. 8. Review every important change. Inspect code diffs, dependency changes, infrastructure modifications, and deployment plans. 9. Protect sensitive information. Never expose API keys, database passwords, access tokens, or confidential application data in prompts or project documentation. 10. Keep humans involved in important decisions. AI agents can accelerate engineering work, but developers remain responsible for architecture, security, quality, and production readiness. 8. Final Thoughts AWS Kiro represents an important direction in AI-assisted software engineering. The real opportunity is not simply asking AI to generate more code. It is using an agent that understands project context, helps define requirements, follows development standards, connects with useful tools, and supports repeatable engineering workflows. Its combination of spec-driven development, steering documents, hooks, MCP integrations, and specialized agent capabilities can help developers approach software development in a more structured way. The AWS Kiro Core workshop is a useful starting point because it brings these concepts together through practical exercises. If you are a software developer, cloud engineer, DevOps engineer, or computer science student, I recommend trying the workshop yourself. Start with a small feature, create its specification, review the design, implement the tasks, and test the result. Let AI help you move faster, but keep engineering decisions, security, and final approval in your hands. References and Further Learning Here are the official resources to explore Kiro in more detail: AWS Kiro Core Workshop Kiro Official Documentation Kiro Official Website AWS Kiro Documentation Overview Kiro — Spec-Driven Development Kiro — Steering Documents Kiro — Hooks Kiro — MCP Integration Kiro — Agent Skills Kiro — Powers Note: Kiro features, availability, and documentation can change. Check the official documentation for the latest information before following a particular setup or configuration procedure. Have you tried agentic development with Kiro? Which capability would make the biggest difference in your daily development workflow: specs, steering, hooks, or MCP? Share your experience in the comments!

  • Code quality checks.

The goal is to make agents more useful for specialized engineering responsibilities.

2.6 Custom Agents and Permissions

Different software development tasks require different responsibilities.

For example:

Agent role Responsibility Code Review Agent Review code changes and identify issues Testing Agent Identify missing tests and validate functionality Infrastructure Agent Review infrastructure configuration Documentation Agent Generate and maintain technical documentation

Custom agents can help organize work around these responsibilities.

Permissions are equally important.

An AI agent should not automatically receive unrestricted access to application files, credentials, databases, or cloud infrastructure.

Developers should configure access carefully and review high-impact operations before execution.

This becomes particularly important when using agents for AWS development and deployment workflows.

3. Kiro IDE, CLI, Web, Mobile, and Crew

Kiro's agent experience extends beyond a traditional code editor.

Depending on availability and product status, developers can explore different Kiro surfaces.

Kiro IDE: An integrated development environment for coding, specifications, steering documents, hooks, and agent workflows.

Kiro CLI: A command-line experience for interacting with agents directly from the terminal.

Kiro Web: A browser-based experience for agent-driven development tasks.

Kiro Mobile: A mobile experience for interacting with development tasks and agent activity. Check the official documentation for current availability and preview status.

Kiro Crew: An agent experience focused on ongoing work, reusable context, and task-oriented workflows.

These experiences provide more flexibility for developers who work across different environments.

Check the official Kiro documentation for the latest feature availability.

4. Vibe Coding vs. Spec-Driven Development

Two useful approaches to building applications with Kiro are vibe coding and spec-driven development.

Vibe Coding

Vibe coding is an interactive approach where developers describe what they want and work with AI to generate or modify code.

Example:

Create a modern student management dashboard.

Include:

- A sidebar.
- A student overview section.
- Student information cards.
- A searchable student table.
- A responsive layout.

Use the existing frontend framework.

This approach is useful for:

  • Quick prototypes.
  • UI improvements.
  • Small features.
  • Experiments.
  • Learning new technologies.
Spec-Driven Development

Spec-driven development starts with requirements and technical planning.

Example:

Build a student search feature.

Requirements:

- Search by name, email, and student ID.
- Filter by course and enrollment status.
- Support pagination.
- Validate user inputs.
- Add automated tests.
- Follow existing authorization rules.

First generate the requirements,
technical design, and implementation tasks.

Wait for my approval before implementation.

This approach is useful for:

  • Complex features.
  • Production applications.
  • Multi-component changes.
  • Team development.
  • Projects with clear acceptance criteria.

Neither approach is universally better. Choose based on the complexity and risk of the task.

5. Hands-On Project: Build a Student Search Feature Using Kiro

Let's apply these concepts in a practical project.

The AWS Kiro Core workshop provides a Student Management Portal learning exercise. We'll use a similar feature to demonstrate how Kiro can help transform a requirement into a working implementation.

Project Objective

Build a feature that allows users to:

  1. Search students by name.
  2. Search students by email.
  3. Search students by student ID.
  4. Filter students by course.
  5. Filter students by enrollment status.
  6. Navigate results using pagination.
  7. See a useful message when no results match.
Step 1: Access the AWS Kiro Core Workshop

Open the official workshop:

https://catalog.us-east-1.prod.workshops.aws/workshops/7aa94656-c586-4ee3-8b5a-5494b3b488b4

Follow the workshop setup instructions and prepare the provided development environment.

The workshop uses an AWS Academy lab environment. Follow its specific IAM and environment restrictions. Do not create additional resources or permissions that the lab does not allow.

Open the Student Management Portal project in Kiro.

Step 2: Ask Kiro to Understand the Existing Application

Before making changes, ask Kiro to analyze the project.

Use this prompt:

Analyze this Student Management Portal project.

I want to understand:

1. The frontend architecture.
2. The backend architecture.
3. The database structure.
4. Existing student-related APIs.
5. Current search and filtering functionality.
6. Authentication and authorization.
7. Existing testing approach.

Identify the files relevant to implementing
a student search and filter feature.

Do not modify any files yet.

Provide a clear summary of the existing
application architecture and development flow.

Expected result:

Kiro should explain the existing project structure and identify the files relevant to the feature.

Review its findings before proceeding.

Step 3: Generate Steering Documents

Ask Kiro to document the project's technical context.

Analyze the existing application and create
project steering documents.

Create:

- product.md
- tech.md
- structure.md

Document:

1. Application purpose.
2. Technology stack.
3. Coding conventions.
4. Project directory structure.
5. Development standards.
6. Testing approach.
7. Security guidelines.

Use the existing project as the source of truth.

Do not invent technologies or change
the existing application architecture.

Expected result:

Kiro should generate project-specific steering documents.

Review the content and correct any inaccurate information.

Step 4: Create the Feature Specification

Now move to spec-driven development.

Use this prompt:

Create a specification for a Student
Search and Filter feature.

Functional requirements:

1. Search students by name.
2. Search students by email.
3. Search students by student ID.
4. Filter students by course.
5. Filter students by enrollment status.
6. Support pagination.
7. Display a message when no students
   match the search.
8. Validate search inputs.
9. Follow existing authentication
   and authorization rules.
10. Add automated tests.

Generate these artifacts:

- requirements.md
- design.md
- tasks.md

Follow the existing application architecture
and project steering documents.

Do not implement the feature yet.

Wait for my review and approval
before making code changes.

Expected result:

Kiro should help produce three specification artifacts.

Review the requirements, design decisions, and implementation tasks.

Check whether important edge cases are covered, including empty search terms, invalid inputs, duplicate records, and unauthorized access.

Step 5: Implement the Feature

After reviewing and approving the specification, ask Kiro to implement it.

Implement the approved Student Search
and Filter specification.

Follow the existing project architecture.

Work through the implementation tasks
in the specified order.

For each task:

1. Explain the planned changes.
2. Implement the required functionality.
3. Add or update automated tests.
4. Run relevant tests.
5. Summarize modified files.
6. Report any errors or limitations.

Do not modify unrelated functionality.

Ask for my approval before any destructive
or high-impact operation.

Expected result:

Kiro should work through the implementation tasks and report the changes.

Review the generated code and diffs rather than accepting every change automatically.

Step 6: Create an Agent Hook

Let's automate part of the development workflow.

Use this prompt:

Create an agent hook that helps maintain
test coverage for the Student Management Portal.

When relevant backend files are modified,
run the appropriate backend test command.

When relevant frontend files are modified,
run the appropriate frontend test command.

Display test failures clearly.

Do not automatically deploy the application.
Do not make unrelated code changes.

Wait for developer review before
applying additional fixes.

Configure the hook according to the actual project structure, available hook events, and test commands.

Expected result:

A reusable automation workflow that helps developers remember to run relevant tests after changes.

Step 7: Explore AWS Documentation Through MCP

Configure the AWS Documentation MCP server by following the official workshop instructions.

Then use this prompt:

I am preparing to deploy this application
on AWS.

Use the available AWS documentation tools
to research suitable deployment options.

Explain:

1. Suitable AWS services.
2. A possible deployment architecture.
3. Security considerations.
4. Networking requirements.
5. Cost considerations.
6. Monitoring and logging options.

Do not create AWS resources
or deploy the application.

Only provide a technical recommendation.

Expected result:

Kiro can use the configured documentation tools to help research relevant AWS services and deployment considerations.

Review all recommendations against official AWS documentation before applying them.

Step 8: Test the Completed Feature

Finally, validate the implementation.

Use this checklist:

  • [ ] Search by student name works.
  • [ ] Search by email works.
  • [ ] Search by student ID works.
  • [ ] Course filtering works.
  • [ ] Enrollment status filtering works.
  • [ ] Pagination works.
  • [ ] Empty search results are handled correctly.
  • [ ] Invalid inputs are handled safely.
  • [ ] Authorization rules are respected.
  • [ ] Automated tests pass.
  • [ ] Existing application functionality still works.
What Have We Learned?

By completing this project, you will understand how to use Kiro for:

  • Understanding an existing codebase.
  • Creating project steering documents.
  • Defining feature requirements.
  • Designing implementation plans.
  • Generating and reviewing code.
  • Automating development checks.
  • Connecting external documentation through MCP.
  • Validating the final implementation.

This is a practical way to move from simply asking AI to generate code toward using an agentic development workflow.

6. How Kiro Can Improve Developer Productivity

Let's connect Kiro's capabilities with common software development challenges.

Development challenge Kiro capability Potential benefit Unclear requirements Spec-driven development Better feature planning Repeating project instructions Steering documents Consistent project context Repetitive development checks Agent Hooks Less manual work Finding external documentation MCP integrations Reduced context switching Repeated specialized workflows Skills and Powers Reusable expertise Different development responsibilities Custom agents Focused workflows Managing agent activity Agent session management Better task visibility Unwanted access to files or tools Permissions More control over agent actions

The biggest opportunity is reducing the time spent switching between planning, coding, documentation, testing, and troubleshooting.

However, productivity should not be measured only by how quickly code is generated.

A better measure is how quickly a developer can deliver a correct, tested, secure, and maintainable feature.

7. Best Practices for Using Kiro in Real Projects

Here are some practical recommendations for developers and engineering teams.

1. Understand the existing codebase first.

Ask Kiro to analyze the application architecture before requesting major changes.

2. Write clear prompts.

Include expected behavior, constraints, validation requirements, and edge cases.

3. Review specifications before implementation.

An incorrect requirement can produce incorrect code. Review the requirements and design before proceeding.

4. Keep steering documents updated.

Outdated technical context can lead to incorrect implementation decisions.

5. Automate repetitive tasks.

Use hooks for routine checks, but keep risky operations under developer control.

6. Apply least-privilege access.

Do not give agents unrestricted access to production environments, credentials, or cloud resources.

7. Test AI-generated code.

Run unit tests, integration tests, security checks, and application-level validation.

8. Review every important change.

Inspect code diffs, dependency changes, infrastructure modifications, and deployment plans.

9. Protect sensitive information.

Never expose API keys, database passwords, access tokens, or confidential application data in prompts or project documentation.

10. Keep humans involved in important decisions.

AI agents can accelerate engineering work, but developers remain responsible for architecture, security, quality, and production readiness.

8. Final Thoughts

AWS Kiro represents an important direction in AI-assisted software engineering.

The real opportunity is not simply asking AI to generate more code. It is using an agent that understands project context, helps define requirements, follows development standards, connects with useful tools, and supports repeatable engineering workflows.

Its combination of spec-driven development, steering documents, hooks, MCP integrations, and specialized agent capabilities can help developers approach software development in a more structured way.

The AWS Kiro Core workshop is a useful starting point because it brings these concepts together through practical exercises.

If you are a software developer, cloud engineer, DevOps engineer, or computer science student, I recommend trying the workshop yourself.

Start with a small feature, create its specification, review the design, implement the tasks, and test the result.

Let AI help you move faster, but keep engineering decisions, security, and final approval in your hands.

References and Further Learning

Here are the official resources to explore Kiro in more detail:

  1. AWS Kiro Core Workshop

  3. Kiro Official Website
  4. AWS Kiro Documentation Overview
  5. Kiro — Spec-Driven Development

Note: Kiro features, availability, and documentation can change. Check the official documentation for the latest information before following a particular setup or configuration procedure.

title: I Built a Healthcare Platform Where AI Is Never Allowed to Have the Final Word.
summary: 🧩 What I Built Healthcare information is dangerously fragmented across short consultations, handwritten prescriptions, laboratory documents, hospital discharge papers, and specialist referrals. To bridge these gaps, I built Diagnosia : a connected healthcare workflow platform that helps clinicians, specialists, patients, and care teams manage information across the entire patient journey. Diagnosia is not a collection of disconnected AI demos. It is a coordinated system where: 📥 Information enters through existing workflows 🤖 AI prepares reviewable drafts 🔐 Authorized modules reuse relevant context 🔄 Workflow events update the patient journey 🛠️ Core Tools The platform is anchored by three foundational tools: Tool Purpose 🎙️ DiagnoFast Voice-first patient intake 🔬 Skin Cancer Detection Image-based screening support 💊 Prescription Analyzer Medication interpretation ➕ Add-On Modules Four focused modules extend this foundation: Module Purpose 📝 ClinScribe Encounter summarization 🧪 LabLens Lab report digitisation 🏥 DischargeCare Transition coordination 🔁 ReferralLoop Specialist tracking 🎬 Demo 📂 View the demo folder on Google Drive The platform's visual identity reflects its underlying clarity , as shown in the UI screenshots in the demo folder. The demo walks through an end-to-end synthetic patient journey on the CareFlow timeline : 🎙️ DiagnoFast captures a voice interview and queues a report 🧪 LabLens digitises a scanned test 📝 ClinScribe drafts a clinical note based entirely on the consultation transcript ⚡ The timeline updates live, without reloading , reflecting every state change 🤝 Partner Technologies Three sponsor technologies were integrated, each with a strictly defined, isolated responsibility to prevent conflicting sources of truth . Partner Role Responsibility ✨ Google Gemini API Multimodal engine Reads scanned lab reports and prescription photos ; outputs are validated against a schema before reaching human review 🗄️ YugabyteDB Technical audit trail Holds all records of AI runs, attempts, and handoffs , keeping the core clinical database clean 🧠 Meko (via MCP server) Shared agent context Manages approved knowledge and memory 🍃 MongoDB Atlas Workflow event store Uses Change Streams to instantly project updates onto open care screens 🏗️ Architecture Principles One responsibility per technology : no sponsor database may override the local identity authority Schema-validated AI output : nothing reaches a reviewer unchecked Event-driven timeline : state changes are projected live via Change Streams Context reuse by authorization : modules only access relevant, permitted context Audit separated from clinical data : technical records never pollute the core clinical database 🔒 Safety Boundaries ✅ Synthetic data only : this is a pilot, not a clinical product ✅ AI output = draft : never final until approved by an authorized human reviewer ✅ Local identity authority is the single source of truth for identity ✅ Schema validation on all multimodal AI outputs ✅ Full audit trail of every AI run, attempt, and handoff 💭 Hackathon Experience Building a modular, feature-frozen product with strict safety boundaries was an incredible test of technical discipline. Wrangling the architecture so that no sponsor database overrode our local identity authority taught me a core lesson: Building for healthcare isn't just about moving fast. It is about meticulously engineering trust. Diagnosia · Connected care, reviewable by design.
summary_html:
🧩 What I Built

Healthcare information is dangerously fragmented across short consultations, handwritten prescriptions, laboratory documents, hospital discharge papers, and specialist referrals.

To bridge these gaps, I built Diagnosia: a connected healthcare workflow platform that helps clinicians, specialists, patients, and care teams manage information across the entire patient journey.

Diagnosia is not a collection of disconnected AI demos. It is a coordinated system where:

  1. 📥 Information enters through existing workflows
  2. 🤖 AI prepares reviewable drafts
  3. 🔐 Authorized modules reuse relevant context
  4. 🔄 Workflow events update the patient journey
🛠️ Core Tools

The platform is anchored by three foundational tools:

Tool Purpose 🎙️ DiagnoFast Voice-first patient intake 🔬 Skin Cancer Detection Image-based screening support 💊 Prescription Analyzer Medication interpretation
➕ Add-On Modules

Four focused modules extend this foundation:

Module Purpose 📝 ClinScribe Encounter summarization 🧪 LabLens Lab report digitisation 🏥 DischargeCare Transition coordination 🔁 ReferralLoop Specialist tracking
🎬 Demo

📂 View the demo folder on Google Drive

The platform's visual identity reflects its underlying clarity, as shown in the UI screenshots in the demo folder.

The demo walks through an end-to-end synthetic patient journey on the CareFlow timeline:

  1. 🎙️ DiagnoFast captures a voice interview and queues a report
  2. 🧪 LabLens digitises a scanned test
  3. 📝 ClinScribe drafts a clinical note based entirely on the consultation transcript
  4. ⚡ The timeline updates live, without reloading, reflecting every state change
🤝 Partner Technologies

Three sponsor technologies were integrated, each with a strictly defined, isolated responsibility to prevent conflicting sources of truth.

Partner Role Responsibility ✨ Google Gemini API Multimodal engine Reads scanned lab reports and prescription photos; outputs are validated against a schema before reaching human review 🗄️ YugabyteDB Technical audit trail Holds all records of AI runs, attempts, and handoffs, keeping the core clinical database clean 🧠 Meko (via MCP server) Shared agent context Manages approved knowledge and memory 🍃 MongoDB Atlas Workflow event store Uses Change Streams to instantly project updates onto open care screens
🏗️ Architecture Principles
  • One responsibility per technology: no sponsor database may override the local identity authority
  • Schema-validated AI output: nothing reaches a reviewer unchecked
  • Event-driven timeline: state changes are projected live via Change Streams
  • Context reuse by authorization: modules only access relevant, permitted context
  • Audit separated from clinical data: technical records never pollute the core clinical database
🔒 Safety Boundaries
  • ✅ Synthetic data only: this is a pilot, not a clinical product
  • ✅ AI output = draft: never final until approved by an authorized human reviewer
  • ✅ Local identity authority is the single source of truth for identity
  • ✅ Schema validation on all multimodal AI outputs
  • ✅ Full audit trail of every AI run, attempt, and handoff
💭 Hackathon Experience

Building a modular, feature-frozen product with strict safety boundaries was an incredible test of technical discipline.

Wrangling the architecture so that no sponsor database overrode our local identity authority taught me a core lesson:

Building for healthcare isn't just about moving fast. It is about meticulously engineering trust.

Diagnosia · Connected care, reviewable by design.

title: How We Built Metis in 7 Hours: Recovering Hidden Decisions from Open-Source Projects
summary: Hackathons are exciting, but the real experience begins when you have to turn an idea into something that actually works. When Hacktoberfest Hack Day started, I was nervous. I wanted to build something meaningful, but choosing the right problem statement felt like the first challenge. After listening to talks from four champions, my excitement grew. Their experiences reminded me that hackathons are about learning, experimenting, and pushing yourself beyond what you already know. At around 6:30 PM, our team, Dot, started exploring the problem statements. After nearly an hour of discussion, we selected Problem Statement 6: Open Source Decision Intelligence and Knowledge Recovery. That decision became the starting point of Mentis. The Problem We Wanted to Solve Open-source projects accumulate years of development activity across GitHub commits, pull requests, issues, and code changes. Among this activity are important updates and changes to the codebase, but keeping track of them can become difficult. Imagine a developer making changes to a parser, improving its performance, fixing bugs, or modifying an existing implementation. After the changes are tested and verified, the commit becomes part of the project's development history. However, understanding what changed and keeping track of verified commits across a repository can still be challenging. As projects grow, developers need a reliable way to monitor commits that have already been verified and understand the changes they represent. Without an organized way to track this information, important updates can become difficult to follow. The problem isn't that developers lack information. It's that keeping track of valuable, verified code changes becomes difficult as repositories grow. We wanted to make that information easier to monitor and access. Introducing Mentis Our team, Dot, decided to build Mentis, a project designed to help developers monitor GitHub commits that have already been verified. The goal was to make it easier to track verified commits from GitHub instead of manually searching through repository activity. We wanted Mentis to help answer one important question: What verified changes have been made to this repository? It was an interesting challenge because it combined repository analysis, information retrieval, backend development, and AI. Building the Product Our tech stack included: Frontend: Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS Backend: Python, FastAPI REST API Database: PostgreSQL We chose this stack to build a full-stack application with a frontend for interacting with Mentis, a REST API for backend communication, and PostgreSQL for structured data storage. Development rarely followed a straight path. We researched the problem, analyzed the repository, explored suitable libraries, and worked on connecting the different components. The frontend needed to communicate with the backend, the backend needed to handle application logic, and the database had to support the information we were working with. With limited time, we focused on the essential parts of the product rather than trying to perfect every feature. The AI Integration Challenge One challenge came during AI integration. We wanted the AI to work with repository information, but it wasn't fetching the backend code as expected. That meant the AI was missing important context required for analysis. It taught us a lesson that sounds simple but matters in real applications: An AI model cannot analyze code that the application has not successfully retrieved and provided. Adding AI is not just about writing a prompt. The entire data flow matters—from accessing repository information to passing the right context into the model. The experience showed us that an AI-powered product depends just as much on reliable backend communication and data retrieval as it does on the model itself. The Midnight Journey As the night progressed, excitement slowly turned into exhaustion. The clock kept moving. Our screens were still open, tasks were unfinished, and the deadline was getting closer. After hours of staring at code and debugging, even simple problems started demanding more concentration. There were moments when we felt completely drained. But whenever we looked at the progress we had made, it reminded us why we were still there. We kept working—fixing problems, making improvements, and bringing the different pieces together. Then came 5:30 AM. After nearly seven hours of work, we finally merged our PR. That moment felt different. It wasn't just another GitHub notification. It represented hours of research, coding, debugging, and teamwork. We had started the evening unsure which problem to choose. Now, we had a product ready to submit. We were exhausted, but seeing our work come together made every hour feel worth it. We submitted Mentis. For a moment, there was relief. The product was in, and we had reached the goal we had been working toward. But the hackathon wasn't over. We shifted straight into presentation preparation. Now we had to explain the problem, demonstrate what we built, and communicate why Mentis mattered. After a night of writing code, we were preparing to tell the story behind it. What I Took Away Hacktoberfest Hack Day taught me that building a product is about much more than implementation. Choosing the right problem, researching the repository, connecting technologies, and working through unexpected failures are all part of development. The AI integration challenge reminded me to understand the complete data pipeline before expecting meaningful results. And the overnight journey showed me what persistence looks like when a deadline is approaching. We started with uncertainty, built Mentis, merged our PR at 5:30 AM, submitted the product, and moved on to preparing our presentation. It wasn't a perfect journey, but it was a real one. At 6:30 PM, we had a problem statement. At 5:30 AM, we had a product. And somewhere between those hours, Team Dot learned what it takes to turn an idea into reality.
summary_html:
Hackathons are exciting, but the real experience begins when you have to turn an idea into something that actually works.

When Hacktoberfest Hack Day started, I was nervous. I wanted to build something meaningful, but choosing the right problem statement felt like the first challenge. After listening to talks from four champions, my excitement grew. Their experiences reminded me that hackathons are about learning, experimenting, and pushing yourself beyond what you already know.

At around 6:30 PM, our team, Dot, started exploring the problem statements.

After nearly an hour of discussion, we selected Problem Statement 6: Open Source Decision Intelligence and Knowledge Recovery.

That decision became the starting point of Mentis.

The Problem We Wanted to Solve

Open-source projects accumulate years of development activity across GitHub commits, pull requests, issues, and code changes.

Among this activity are important updates and changes to the codebase, but keeping track of them can become difficult.

Imagine a developer making changes to a parser, improving its performance, fixing bugs, or modifying an existing implementation. After the changes are tested and verified, the commit becomes part of the project's development history.

However, understanding what changed and keeping track of verified commits across a repository can still be challenging.

As projects grow, developers need a reliable way to monitor commits that have already been verified and understand the changes they represent.

Without an organized way to track this information, important updates can become difficult to follow.

The problem isn't that developers lack information. It's that keeping track of valuable, verified code changes becomes difficult as repositories grow.

We wanted to make that information easier to monitor and access.

Introducing Mentis

Our team, Dot, decided to build Mentis, a project designed to help developers monitor GitHub commits that have already been verified.

The goal was to make it easier to track verified commits from GitHub instead of manually searching through repository activity.

We wanted Mentis to help answer one important question:

What verified changes have been made to this repository?

It was an interesting challenge because it combined repository analysis, information retrieval, backend development, and AI.

Building the Product

Our tech stack included:

Frontend: Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS

Backend: Python, FastAPI REST API

Database: PostgreSQL

We chose this stack to build a full-stack application with a frontend for interacting with Mentis, a REST API for backend communication, and PostgreSQL for structured data storage.

Development rarely followed a straight path. We researched the problem, analyzed the repository, explored suitable libraries, and worked on connecting the different components.

The frontend needed to communicate with the backend, the backend needed to handle application logic, and the database had to support the information we were working with.

With limited time, we focused on the essential parts of the product rather than trying to perfect every feature.

The AI Integration Challenge

One challenge came during AI integration.

We wanted the AI to work with repository information, but it wasn't fetching the backend code as expected. That meant the AI was missing important context required for analysis.

It taught us a lesson that sounds simple but matters in real applications:

An AI model cannot analyze code that the application has not successfully retrieved and provided.

Adding AI is not just about writing a prompt. The entire data flow matters—from accessing repository information to passing the right context into the model.

The experience showed us that an AI-powered product depends just as much on reliable backend communication and data retrieval as it does on the model itself.

The Midnight Journey

As the night progressed, excitement slowly turned into exhaustion.

The clock kept moving. Our screens were still open, tasks were unfinished, and the deadline was getting closer. After hours of staring at code and debugging, even simple problems started demanding more concentration.

There were moments when we felt completely drained. But whenever we looked at the progress we had made, it reminded us why we were still there.

We kept working—fixing problems, making improvements, and bringing the different pieces together.

Then came 5:30 AM.

After nearly seven hours of work, we finally merged our PR.

That moment felt different.

It wasn't just another GitHub notification. It represented hours of research, coding, debugging, and teamwork.

We had started the evening unsure which problem to choose. Now, we had a product ready to submit.

We were exhausted, but seeing our work come together made every hour feel worth it.

We submitted Mentis.

For a moment, there was relief. The product was in, and we had reached the goal we had been working toward.

But the hackathon wasn't over.

We shifted straight into presentation preparation. Now we had to explain the problem, demonstrate what we built, and communicate why Mentis mattered.

After a night of writing code, we were preparing to tell the story behind it.

What I Took Away

Hacktoberfest Hack Day taught me that building a product is about much more than implementation.

Choosing the right problem, researching the repository, connecting technologies, and working through unexpected failures are all part of development.

The AI integration challenge reminded me to understand the complete data pipeline before expecting meaningful results.

And the overnight journey showed me what persistence looks like when a deadline is approaching.

We started with uncertainty, built Mentis, merged our PR at 5:30 AM, submitted the product, and moved on to preparing our presentation.

It wasn't a perfect journey, but it was a real one.

At 6:30 PM, we had a problem statement. At 5:30 AM, we had a product. And somewhere between those hours, Team Dot learned what it takes to turn an idea into reality.

title: Lumbre: a Día de los Muertos altar that only remembers what you tell it
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built Lumbre is a small altar for Día de los Muertos. You write the name of someone you want to remember, how you knew them, the years if you know them, one memory, and any food, song, or object that belongs with them. An open-weight model writes the line that sits on the altar and a short remembrance. The memory you typed is kept word for word, under "As told." The food, the song, and the object come from the form. A field you leave blank stays blank. The model is told not to invent a date, a relative, or a favorite thing you did not give it. I read the week as remembrance rather than a jump scare. Día de los Muertos is the thin place between someone who is gone and the people who still set a place for them. The altar is that place: paper, a candle, marigolds, and only the facts you actually brought. You can save the card as a JSON file. Demo https://ashraf01k-lumbre.static.hf.space A card comes back in a few seconds. Use "Try a fictional altar" if you want to see the page before you write a real name. The host allows about two cards a minute. Code https://github.com/AshrafGalaxy/lumbre AshrafGalaxy / lumbre Lumbre Lumbre letters a Día de los Muertos altar card. You write a name, a memory, and only the foods, songs, and objects you actually know. Llama 3.3 70B, an open-weight model, writes the lines on the card. Anything you leave blank stays blank. The memory you typed is kept word for word. The offering list is built in code from those fields, so the model cannot add a favorite food you never named. Why open weights Llama 3.3's weights are public. The altar calls that model on a host, so a card comes back in a few seconds and the page does not download hundreds of megabytes. The model id is one constant, so it can be swapped for another open instruct model. A closed API would lock the wording to one vendor. Architecture flowchart TD visitor[Visitor] --> page[Altar page] page --> facts[Altar facts] facts --> scribe[Scribe] scribe --> … View on GitHub How I Built It The public page is static HTML. Pressing "Light the altar" sends the note once to Llama 3.3 70B Instruct , an open-weight model from Meta, through OVHcloud's OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The browser does not download the weights, and the page does not contain an API key. summary_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Lumbre is a small altar for Día de los Muertos. You write the name of someone you want to remember, how you knew them, the years if you know them, one memory, and any food, song, or object that belongs with them.

An open-weight model writes the line that sits on the altar and a short remembrance. The memory you typed is kept word for word, under "As told." The food, the song, and the object come from the form. A field you leave blank stays blank. The model is told not to invent a date, a relative, or a favorite thing you did not give it.

I read the week as remembrance rather than a jump scare. Día de los Muertos is the thin place between someone who is gone and the people who still set a place for them. The altar is that place: paper, a candle, marigolds, and only the facts you actually brought.

You can save the card as a JSON file.

Demo

https://ashraf01k-lumbre.static.hf.space

A card comes back in a few seconds. Use "Try a fictional altar" if you want to see the page before you write a real name. The host allows about two cards a minute.

Code

https://github.com/AshrafGalaxy/lumbre

AshrafGalaxy / lumbre
Lumbre

Lumbre letters a Día de los Muertos altar card. You write a name, a memory, and only the foods, songs, and objects you actually know. Llama 3.3 70B, an open-weight model, writes the lines on the card. Anything you leave blank stays blank.

The memory you typed is kept word for word. The offering list is built in code from those fields, so the model cannot add a favorite food you never named.

Why open weights

Llama 3.3's weights are public. The altar calls that model on a host, so a card comes back in a few seconds and the page does not download hundreds of megabytes. The model id is one constant, so it can be swapped for another open instruct model. A closed API would lock the wording to one vendor.

Architecture

    page --> facts[Altar facts]
    facts --> scribe[Scribe]
    scribe -->
…
View on GitHub
How I Built It

The public page is static HTML. Pressing "Light the altar" sends the note once to Llama 3.3 70B Instruct, an open-weight model from Meta, through OVHcloud's OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The browser does not download the weights, and the page does not contain an API key.

The scribe is small on purpose. lumbre/prompts.py asks for two labeled parts, an inscription and a remembrance. lumbre/altar.py builds the offering list and the list of gaps from the fields you filled in. The model is not trusted to decide what was brought to the altar.

Gemma is open-weight too, and the weights are on Hugging Face. I did not use it for the live card. The Hugging Face router can serve Gemma, but this account has no Inference Providers credits, and a free account cannot run a Docker Space to load the weights. The host that answers with no key does not offer a Gemma chat model. Llama 3.3 70B is the open chat model that host does serve, so that is what letters the card. The model id is one constant.

A remembrance should not depend on a closed chat product that can change its model or shut the endpoint down. Llama's weights are public. Lumbre calls that model by name, and the same scribe can point at another open instruct model. The offering list is ordinary code, so a model update cannot quietly add a favorite food. The note is sent for one reply. Lumbre does not keep a database of it.

title: A ChatGPT share link leaked your private conversations
summary: In October 2026, a research team at parameter.ai turned an ordinary public ChatGPT share link into attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it. The victim only had to open the link. There was no app to install, no project to join, no code to paste, no developer tools. OpenAI classified the report as P1 and shipped a fix on October 26. The payload ran as chatgpt.com, which is the part that matters. From there it enumerated the victim's conversation list, pulled the content of a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and sent selected data to an external server. It called ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, so its reach was whatever the normal frontend can do on your account. The chain is worth walking through because no single piece of it was broken. A graph and a preview ChatGPT's Preview feature renders an HTML code block as a working page. Since that HTML can contain anything, ChatGPT runs it inside a restricted frame on a separate web address. The browser treats the Preview as a different site, so code inside it cannot read parent.document or otherwise inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it. That isolation held. Preview code could not reach the parent directly. The same conversation also contained an interactive graph. Rendering it loaded a math library, MathLive. Loading MathLive did one extra thing: it installed a postMessage listener in the main ChatGPT page to handle its on-screen keyboard. postMessage is the sanctioned way for two frames to talk when the browser won't let them read each other's pages. It is safe only if the receiver checks who sent the message. MathLive's top-level controller used an origin policy of none, so it accepted messages from any origin, and it did not require the setting-change message to come from a window it had previously approved. The graph installed the receiver; the sandboxed Preview supplied a sender nobody had vetted. HTML into the parent The Preview sent two messages. The first replaced a virtual-keyboard layout with the attacker's HTML, since MathLive allowed keyboard layouts to contain raw markup. The second told MathLive to show the keyboard, which joined the layout into an HTML string and assigned it to innerHTML in the real ChatGPT page. A helper called createHTML looked like it might sanitize that string. It was an identity Trusted Types wrapper: it marked the string as trusted and passed it through unchanged. Trusted Types can control who writes to an HTML sink, but an identity policy doesn't make an attacker's string safe. innerHTML alone doesn't execute script; tags injected that way stay inert. The layout therefore inserted an iframe with a srcdoc attribute, and MathLive added that frame to the main document with no sandbox attribute. srcdoc forces a fresh HTML parse, which gives an external script somewhere to run, and because the main chatgpt.com page created the frame, the browser handed the new document the chatgpt.com origin. Code inside it could now read the parent. Getting script past CSP Content Security Policy blocked inline JavaScript, as it should. It did allow scripts from YouTube. YouTube's oEmbed endpoint supports a JSONP-style callback parameter, and JSONP responses are JavaScript, not JSON. The endpoint rejected invalid callbacks, but it wrote the callback into the response body before appending its validation error. Ending the callback with ;void turned the trailing error object into a no-op. The response came back HTTP 200 with Content-Type text/javascript and nosniff set, and since YouTube was on the CSP allowlist, the browser loaded it as a script and ran the callback inside the unsandboxed frame. That produced arbitrary JavaScript executing as chatgpt.com. Google rewrites angle brackets in the callback, so the payload used classic function syntax rather than arrow functions to survive the round trip. From lab bug to one link The first working version used a researcher-controlled ChatGPT App as the message sender, which meant a victim would have to connect or invoke that app first. A native HTML attachment removed that step, since ChatGPT opened the attachment in the same sandboxed Preview. But exporting the conversation as a public share kept the attachment and dropped the graph, and the graph was what loaded MathLive and installed the vulnerable listener. The attachment could still send the two messages, but nothing in the parent was listening. The working approach put both halves in one ordinary public conversation: a genuine graph to initialize MathLive in the main page, and a later assistant-authored HTML Preview to send the messages. The resulting /share/ link carried the whole chain to anyone who opened it, deliverable by email, chat, a support ticket, or a social post. Because the graph and Preview loaded independently, the payload sometimes fired before MathLive was ready, so the carrier retried the two messages for a short window, with a guard in the parent so the data-theft step ran only once. In the most stable reproduction the victim clicked Preview once; marking the HTML block as previewable made ChatGPT open it automatically, reducing the whole thing to a single click on the link. The automatic path reproduced three times in a separate account, including after a hard refresh, with the proof alert appearing around 4.5 seconds in. What the code actually did An alert proves where code runs, not why it matters. The same-origin frame parsed #client-bootstrap out of the parent document, pulled the session access token and account ID, and checked that the account ID in the token matched the session when both were present. It then set its own headers and called the real APIs: GET /backend-api/conversations?...&limit=20ℴ=updated&offset=0 GET /backend-api/conversations/ ?num_turns=2 A 403, 404, or 405 on the detail request fell back to the legacy /backend-api/conversation/?include_full_conversation=true route. This is authenticated API access, not screen scraping. The target conversation had no relationship to the malicious share. The response left over an ordinary image request to the attacker's server, after the code cleared its references to the token, account, and headers. The team sent only a small slice of the response off-site; the injected code already held the full authenticated reply and could have taken anything the frontend can reach. What OpenAI fixed, and what to take from it The Preview sandbox itself was fine. The problem was a privileged component in the main page willing to act on the sandbox's instructions. OpenAI reproduced both the script execution and the private-conversation read, rolled the fix across two versions of the web frontend, and on October 26 confirmed both versions reject the cross-frame MathLive messages. During the rollout a CSP change blocked part of the original chain while one version still needed the real fix, which is a fair reminder that CSP was a speed bump here, not the wall. If you build anything with a shareable or embeddable surface, the pattern generalizes. A postMessage receiver has to check both event.origin and event.source before acting on a state-changing message; neither alone is enough. Settings passed between windows should not carry raw HTML. A dynamically created document whose contents can be influenced by an untrusted frame should keep its sandbox attribute, so a fresh document can't inherit your origin. CSP belongs behind those controls as defense in depth, because an allowlisted third party with a JSONP endpoint is a script source you don't control. The bug lived in the seams. Preview was isolated, graphs could load a keyboard, frames could exchange messages, CSP allowed a major media host, and conversations could be shared. Each was reasonable alone. Treating every public share as attacker-controlled input would have caught the combination that wasn't.
